747513968: The Grab Sensor produces a signal when the object it’s placed on is grabbed. Find one on the Creatures & Characters page of your Tools Bag and set it down on a sponge with the action button. See how it lights up when you grab the sponge? You can attach the sensor’s signal to trigger any logic you like. Like most things, the Grab Sensor can be tweaked. Just hover the popit cursor over it and press the menu button to open its tweak menu. If you activate the Require All Players tweak, the Grab Sensor will only produce a signal when every player in your level is grabbing the object. Use the Character to Detect tweak to open the Character menu and select a specific character for the Grab Sensor to require. If you change your mind, just use the Reset button! The options in the Movinator Cursor category use features unique to the Move Pack DLC. If you own the Move Pack, you can learn about them there! Finally, you can invert the Grab Sensor’s output so that grabbing it turns its signal off instead of on!

1646421298: The Game Ender allows you to put a stop to a level using logic! Find one on the Gameplay page of your Tools Bag and use the action button to place it in the world.  In Play Mode, once the Game Ender is triggered by a button, a sensor, or any other logic, the level will come to an end. If your level has a Scoreboard, all the players will be teleported to it instantly. If there is no Scoreboard, they will simply see the Continue or Replay menu instead.  If you deactivate the Success tweak, the Game Ender will not send players to the Scoreboard – it will just send them to the menu no matter what. Activating the Ends Adventure tweak will allow players to rate your adventure!
2267119669: The Creatinator is a powerup that lets a Sackthing fire objects from a cannon on its head. You can let your players fire anything from a Creatinator! Grab one now from the Creatures & Characters page of your Tools Bag, then place it in the world with the action button. Just run across the Creatinator to pick it up and press the grab button to fire it. By default, a Creatinator fires a stream of water, but we can easily change this by using the popit cursor and the menu button to open the Creatinator’s tweak menu. Use the Object to Emit tweak to select from your Collected Objects page, an assortment of projectiles and explosives from the Gameplay page, or things you’ve made yourself on the My Objects page. Highlight your choice and press the action button, then position and reshape the object using the left and right sticks. Once you’ve positioned the object where you want it to emit from the Creatinator, just press the action button. Adjust the Ammo tweak to give your Creatinator a limited number of shots. Use the Max Emitted at Once tweak to change how many shots can onscreen at the same time. Activate the Recycle Old Objects tweak if you want new objects to replace old ones as they’re emitted. Change the Linear Velocity tweak to make the object launch faster or slower and use the Angular Velocity tweak to give it some spin. If you want a Creatinator to have a bit of randomness to its direction, lower the Accuracy tweak! Change the Rate of Fire tweak to change the delay between shots. The Lifetime tweak determines how long your shots last in the world after they’re fired. Use the Visual Style tweak to change what the Creatinator itself looks like on your Sackthing’s head, and the Create and Destroy Effects to change how the shots look when they appear and vanish. Finally, if you don’t want a player to be able to get rid of the Creatinator, be sure to turn off the Can Be Dropped tweak!

3268658563: The Popit Cursor Sensor is used in conjunction with the Popit Powerup. It outputs a signal when the player’s popit cursor interacts with the object it’s placed on. It’s a helpful tool for building your own Popit related gameplay! It’s on the Creatures & Characters page of your Tools Bag, so slap one down and take a look. You can easily see the Popit Cursor Sensor in action in Create. Just hover your popit cursor over the object you placed it on and observe as it lights up. Simple! Of course, there are tweaks to play with. Open up the tweak menu using the menu button. The first tweak is the Trigger On tweak. By default, it’s on Hover, which means it will activate when you hover your popit cursor over the object. If you set it to Picked Up instead, the sensor will activate only once you pick the object up using the popit cursor. With the Include Gadgets tweak you can control whether the Popit Cursor Sensor will also output a signal when players interact with attached logic, attached connectors, or both.  If your object is one small piece of a larger whole, the Include Rigid Connections tweak allows you to treat it all as one big object. Finally, you can invert the Popit Cursor Sensor’s output just like any other output.

2132965346: Decorations are like Stickers, but in three fabulous dimensions! Sprinkle them throughout your levels to give your players something pretty to gawk at. All your Decorations are stored on the Decorations page of your Stickers & Decorations, so scroll through them and find one you like to learn how they work. Highlight your choice and press the action button to pull it out. A Decoration cannot be placed on its own – it needs somewhere to sit! You can place them on materials, objects, and even Sackthings! Just position your Decoration using the left stick, spin it and resize it with the right stick, and pop it down with the action button. Then just back out of the menu using the back button and admire your handiwork. If you misplace a Decoration or just change your mind about it altogether, you need to use the Sticker & Decoration Edit Tool. It lives at the top of your Sticker & Decorations menu. Select it with the action button now.  Move your cursor back to the Decoration you placed and press the action button. You’ve snatched it up again, and can move it wherever you like! Finally, you can also use the Sticker & Decoration Edit Tool to delete decorations altogether – just press the delete button. You don’t even need to select it first!

There’s the normal Checkpoint, which allows your players four lives before their game ends. The Double-Life Checkpoint gives them eight. The Infinite-Life Checkpoint provides an endless stream of lives for your players to expend! Other than that, all three Checkpoints function the same way, so just pick your favorite and open its tweak menu with the left stick and the menu button. With the Entrance Type tweak, determine whether the Checkpoint is for everyone or for specific teams. You can also set it to Last Activated if you only want it to function for players who personally activate it. If you’re feeling extra stingy, the Copy from Previous tweak allows you to preserve the number of lives remaining from Checkpoint to Checkpoint!  Finally, you can tweak the appearance of your Checkpoint and whether it makes noise to make sure it fits in with its surroundings.

173016930: The Music Objects are used to fill your levels with melodious music! You can find them, appropriately enough, on the Music page of your Tools Bag. Highlighting them in the menu will play a little preview of the song, so find one you like the sound of and place it in the world with the action button. By default, a Music Object is triggered by player proximity, so just wander over to it and the song will begin to play! You can also trigger a Music Object via logic – just wire something into its input. Now open up the Music Object’s tweak menu using the menu button. You can adjust the volume of the song with the Track Volume tweak. You can adjust the point in the song that the Music Object will start playing from by changing the Start Point tweak! If your Music Object is triggered via player proximity, use the Trigger Radius and Layer Detection Range tweaks to change how close a player needs to be to activate it. Finally, there’s a special type of Music Object called an Interactive Track. When tweaking one of these, you’ll see that there are multiple stems for you to play around with.! With these, you can customize which instruments are playing at any given time. Have some fun with it!

4065066288: The Dynamic Thermometer gives you lots of extra room in your level. Unfortunately it doesn’t give you infinite thermometer. To ensure your level runs smoothly, it is very important that you do not have lots and lots of things being loaded at once. The best way to do this is to carefully manage your loading zones. We’ll go over some tips and tricks to help manage your loading zones allowing you to increase performance on your dynamic thermometer levels. As a general rule, you want your loading zones to be as compact as possible. There are a couple of things you can do to achieve this. When creating in a Dynamic Thermometer level, you will want to avoid gluing things as much as possible. Larger objects like floors and platforms are especially best left unglued. They can often create large loading zones and cause unnecessary stuff to stream in. Instead, make objects either static or use the Anti-Gravity Tweaker to keep things in place. Another thing you want to pay special attention to when creating a dynamic thermometer level is the radii of your sensors. As the radius of a sensor gets larger, so does its loading zone. In Dynamic Thermometer levels, you should always try to shrink down the radius of your sensor as much as possible. Additionally, you can also tweak the Trigger Angle Range to shrink down the loading zone even further. One of the biggest trouble makers in Dynamic Thermometer Levels are long logic wires. Remember, connecting two objects or logic pieces with a wire will put them in the same loading zone. If the objects are far apart from each other, this loading zone will be very large and may cause things to load in when it’s not needed. Here, the button on the bottom left of our level is connected with a wire to a teleporter on the top right of the level. Because the resulting loading zone has the shape of a large rectangle around all objects in the zone, the loading zone will include the area in the centre. This means that when the player is in the centre, both the bottom left and the top right area of the level will get loaded into our streaming zone. As Sackboy is nowhere near these areas, loading these parts of the level while Sackboy is in the centre is a waste of resources. This can possibly affect the performance of the level. It’s best to prevent this kind of setup whenever possible, so we will delete the wire causing the issue. As you can see, unplugging the wire removed the large loading zone and left us with three nice compact zones. So how do we get the signal from the button to the Teleporter without creating a huge loading zone? Remember, using a normal tag sensor to transmit the signal wirelessly would create a very large radius, which also creates a large loading zone. This is why we will use the Remote Tag Sensor. Because this sensor does not have a radius, it does not create a loading zone in the same way as a normal sensor would. First, plug the button into a Tag. Then grab a Remote Tag Sensor from the Sensors section of the Tools Bag and hook it up to the Teleporter. Now comes the tricky part. If we press the button, nothing happens! This is because the remote tag sensor is not loaded in while we are in this section of the level. The solution here is to use a Preloader to make sure that the remote tag sensor is loaded in when we are about to press the button. Grab a Preloader from your tools bag and place it near the button. Now, open its tweak menu. Select Place Zone and move the box over to the Teleporter area. Set it to Full Load and tweak the maximum detection range so it covers the button. You also want to make sure it has a correct layer range. By doing this, the destination area and remote tag sensor load in your level whenever a player is close to the button. This makes the area ready for someone to teleport to! As you can see, the teleporter works again! Plus we still have our three separate loading zones. Now you can be in the centre without the rest of the level loading in. Use this technique whenever you can to replace long wires. Your dynamic thermometer levels will run even better! If you ever want to know exactly what is being loaded in in a certain area, you can use the Lock Dynamic Loading option from the Start menu. When you enable this, all dynamic loading will pause and you can fly around to see what is currently being loaded in. This feature can be very useful to identify areas of your level where too much stuff gets loaded in. To see how this works, let’s see if this level really has separate the loading zones. If we enable Lock Dynamic Loading while in the centre of the level, we can see that both corners of the level are indeed not loaded in. We can also check to see if our Preloader works, too. Let’s land near the button that teleports the player, lock dynamic loading, then check to see if the destination is indeed being loaded in. As you can see, our new setup works beautifully! Another way to gain more information about your loading zones is to zoom the camera out until you start seeing colored boxes. This view is called the Streaming Visualizer. As you fly around your level in this view, active loading zones become visible, while loading zones that are currently stored in memory will show up as red boxes. If you have set up your dynamic thermometer level correctly, only parts of the level close to Sackboy will be visible. The rest of the level should show up red. You can also combine this view with Lock Dynamic Loading to see what is currently loaded in. Areas that are currently loaded in will show up as green, like our preloaded teleporter setup. Objects that have permanency tweakers will also show up as green as well.

301990223: Emitters are used to add things to the world that weren’t previously there! You can emit anything from projectiles to entire buildings. Find one on the Gadgets page of your Tools Bag and let’s get to know them! Just place it in the world with the popit cursor and the action button. First, your Emitter needs something to emit. Open up the Emitter’s tweak menu using the menu button, then select Choose Object. From there, you can choose from things like projectiles and explosives on the Gameplay page, objects you’ve created yourself on your My Objects page, and any of the objects on your Collected Objects page. You can also use the Pick Emitted Object option to emit a copy of a reference object in the world. Let’s select that option now. Position the capture box over the object you want to emit using the left stick. If you need to reshape the box, use the right stick. Once you have the object selected, press the action button. Notice that you now have a faded copy of the object that you can reposition and reorient. This is where and how the object will emit. Place it however you like, and then press the action button. If you back out of the tweak menu with the back button, you can see the Emitter take effect! The object appears in the world over and over again. Of course there are plenty more tweaks for this behavior, so enter the tweak menu again. Activate the Reference in Play Mode tweak if you want player-induced changes to the reference object, such as stickers, to appear on the emitted versions. Turn it off to keep the emitted versions all the same. Use the Linear Velocity tweak to make the object launch out of the emitter at any speed you like, and the Angular Velocity tweak to give it some spin. If the emitter itself is moving and you don’t want its motion to affect the object’s motion, activate the Ignore Parent Velocity tweak. Use the Input Action tweak to change how the Emitter reacts to logic. You can simply turn it on and off, make it emit once per signal, or make it emit faster or slower! The Frequency tweak controls how often the object emits and the Lifetime tweak controls how long each object lasts. If you want it to last forever, you can make it infinite by making it below zero. Use the Sync tweak to change an emitter’s timing relative to the rest of the timing in your level. The Max Emitted tweak controls how many times the Emitter emits before it runs out, and the Max Emitted At Once controls how many objects can be emitted at a time. Activate the Destroy Oldest When Max Emitted Reached tweak to replace the oldest object with the newest object once it hits its limit. The Create and Destroy Effect tweaks change how the object looks when it’s emitted and destroyed. A few final things. The Emit by Zone option in the Choose Object menu allows you to select an entire section of your level to emit, no matter what occupies the area at the time. And lastly, you may have noticed the Destroy All input. When the Emitter receives a signal through this input, all objects it’s emitted are instantly destroyed!

4250002738: A Tag Sensor produces a signal when it detects the tag it’s looking for. Grab one from the Gadgets page of your Tools Bag and place it in the world. Grab a Tag, too, so we can check out how it all works! Observe how the Tag Sensor lights up when you shove the Tag near it, then turns off again when you take the Tag away. That’s the Tag Sensor at its very simplest! Naturally, there are plenty more options in the Tag Sensor’s tweak menu. Open it up now using the popit cursor and the menu button. In the range category, there’s a whole pack of tweaks for changing the Tag Sensor’s detection radius. This radius determines how close a Tag needs to be before the Tag Sensor notices it, so it’s pretty important! You can make the range bigger or smaller, change its angular shape, and change how many layers it can see. You can also tell it whether it can see Tags that share its Microchip! The Number of Keys Required tweak lets you determine how many Tags the Tag Sensor needs to detect before it produces a signal. The Tag Color and Tag Label tweaks let you set up which Tag the Tag Sensor is looking for. If you invert the Tag Sensor’s output, it will start producing a signal when it isn’t detecting a Tag instead.  The Output Value tweak changes the way the strength of the Tag Sensor’s output is calculated. If you just want the Tag Sensor to turn on and off, you can ignore this, but if you need analogue output values, this is the tweak for you! You can determine the Tag Sensor’s output based on the Tag’s closeness, the signal strength of the Tag itself, or the percentage of Tags it can see relative to its required count. Tricky stuff, but worth playing with! Finally, the Show Radii in Play Mode tweak makes a Tag Sensor’s detection range visible to players. This is especially useful for making your own Popit Puzzles!

3104022747: The Global Gameplay Controls can be tweaked to change the way your level plays. Let’s take a peek.  The Game Mode setting controls whether a level is a normal cooperative level, a competitive versus level, or a cutscene. The manual jump down setting controls whether Sackboy can drop from one layer down to a layer beneath him or whether this action is disabled.  You can enable or disable the sackpocket depending on the needs of your level, and the same goes for the Organisertron. If your level doesn’t need them, go ahead and disable them! If your level needs a certain amount of players, you can indicate this to players using the recommended players options. You can set a minimum recommended number, a maximum recommended number or both. It’s worth noting, though, that players will be able to ignore these recommendations and enter a level with any number of sackfolk. In the Game End Conditions options, you can set a level to complete once a certain amount of time passes or once a player accumulates a certain amount of points. If your level has a scoreboard, your players will be moved there automatically. Otherwise, the level will simply stop.  Lower the gravity to let things get nice and floaty. Or turn it up to keep stuff low to the ground. Set the water level as high as you like. When the water level is higher than zero, more water options will appear. Tweaking the wave height will make the water level bob up and down.  If you want to customise the water’s appearance, you can change its colour, make it murky, fill it with bits or toggle the light patterns on and off. The Water Drain Sounds tweak determines whether the water drains noisily or silently. With the Global Gameplay Controls, you can make your level play exactly how you want. Have fun!

1521172773: The Decoration Mount is used to stretch and smoosh decorations. It’s a powerful tool for creating amazing visuals in your levels. Let’s give it a try. If you place a decoration onto the mount, you’ll see the effects immediately. As you can see, the decoration begins stretching back and forth in every direction. Of course, you can tweak how much it stretches on any axis, from left to right with the x axis… up and down with the y axis… or in and out with the z axis.  Now onto the timing tweaks. With the Time tweak, you can choose the duration of each stretch. With the Pause tweak, you can select how long it should pause between each stretch. If you don’t want it to pause at all, just keep it at zero. The Sync tweak allows you to change when the stretches begin and end relative to the rest of the timing in your level. Change the Input Action to determine how the Decoration Mount reacts to logic. Notice that the Decoration Mount has three inputs – one for each axis. You can use any, all, or none of these inputs as you like. The Scale From Top tweak changes whether the decoration will stretch from the center of the Decoration Mount or the top. Finally, if the decoration you’re using is color tweakable, the visuals options will allow you to customize its appearance. You can change its color and its brightness.  With these options you’ll be able to shape decorations into anything you can imagine!

1431128339: The Speed Sensor produces a signal when the object it’s placed on is travelling at a certain speed. Take one from the Gadgets page of your Tools Bag and place it onto an object using the action button. See how the Speed Sensor lights up once the object picks up speed? You can use that signal to trigger any logic you like. Naturally, this behavior can be tweaked! Just hover the popit cursor over the Speed Sensor and press the menu button to open its tweak menu. The Maximum Speed tweak changes the speed necessary for the Speed Sensor to activate. The lower it is, the slower the object needs to go before the Speed Sensor kicks in! Use the Directions tweak to only detect movement in a certain direction. For example, if you select Left, the Speed Sensor will only light up when the object is going left. You can even set it up to trigger based on movement in and out of the layers! 3321816100: The Gameplay Sequencer allows you to set up logic that triggers in a precise order over a precise amount of time. You can find it on the Gadgets page of your Tools Bag, so grab one now and put it into the world with the action button. Right away you’ll see the Gameplay Sequencer open up, revealing a panel of alternating stripes of dark and light colours. Each of these stripes represents a length of time as the Gameplay Sequencer plays from left to right. By default, each stripe lasts one second. By default, a Gameplay Sequencer is triggered by player proximity, so wander over to it to activate it. The line that travels along the panel will activate any logic it meets along the way! Place some logic onto the panel now. You can even stretch most logic across the panel by pushing up on the right stick. Activate the Gameplay Sequencer again to observe the magic. Of course, this isn’t all you can do. Open the Gameplay Sequencer’s tweak menu with the menu button and take a peek.  If you’re going to trigger the Gameplay Sequencer using player proximity, you can adjust its awareness radius with the Trigger Radius and Layer Detection Range tweaks. Otherwise these tweaks can be ignored. If you’re going to trigger it with logic instead, the Input Action will control how the Gameplay Sequencer activates. You can play it forwards or backwards, turn it on and off, adjust how fast it goes, and more. Just hook up some logic to the Gameplay Sequencer’s leftmost input. The Seconds per stripe tweak changes how long it takes for the Gameplay Sequencer to play a stripe. Activate the Loop tweak and the Gameplay Sequencer will start itself over again once it reaches the end of its sequence! You can also change the shape of the panel itself. Exit the tweak menu with the back button, and then select the panel with the action button. Now you can move it around with the left stick, or change its shape with the right stick. Up and down control how tall it is, and left and right control how wide it is. Once that’s sorted, just press the action button again.  Finally, the rightmost input of the Gameplay Sequencer is used to interrupt the sequence and reset it. Use this if you need a way to make the Gameplay Sequencer stop early!

You can speed the bolt up or slow it down with the Speed tweak, and you can change which way it spins using the Direction tweak. The Strength tweak controls the force behind the spinning. 93922199: Buttons and Switches are nice, simple, easily recognizable ways for players to interact with things in your levels. Each of them has an output that can be wired to any logic you like. Find them on the Gameplay page of your Tools Bag and place one of each in the world using the action button. A Button only produces a signal when something is weighing it down. Wire it up to something, and then observe how it turns on and off as you jump up and down on the Button. Simple! The 2-Way Switch has no signal while it’s pointed one way and a constant signal when it’s pointed the other way. Wire it up to something and turn it on by grabbing it and pulling it to the right. Now it will keep sending its signal nonstop until you pull it to the left again! The 3-Way Switch sends a negative signal when it’s pointed one way and a positive signal when it’s pointed the other way. Wire it up to a forwards/backwards motor bolt and pull it back and forth – see how it spins one way, then the other?  Finally, each of these outputs can be reversed from their tweak menus. Just open up the tweak menu with the menu button and activate the Invert Output tweak. Now on is off, off is on, and positive is negative!

3751016568: A Winch is a string-like connection between two objects that can get longer and shorter. They’re on the Gameplay page of the Tools Bag, so navigate to them with the left stick and select them with the action button. To place a connector, use the left stick to move your popit cursor to the surface of an object or material until you see it highlighted, and then press the action button to place the base. Then move your popit cursor to another surface and press the action button to place the other end. Now your two surfaces are connected! Notice how the Winch contracts and expands, moving the lower object up and down. You can also shove the object around as it moves, because the Winch isn’t stiff.  Let’s tweak the Winch by moving the popit cursor over it and pressing the menu button. The first tweak you’ll see is the Maximum Length tweak, which controls how long the Winch can get. Similarly, the Minimum Length tweak sets up the Winch when it’s at its shortest. Adjust the Time tweak to change how long it takes for the Winch to stretch from its minimum to its maximum length and back. If you want it to pause for a while at each end, use the Pause tweak. To sync its timing relative to the rest of the timing in your level, use the Sync tweak! The Strength tweak controls how hard the Winch tries to pull when it’s met with resistance. At 0% it won’t even move at all, the lazy thing. The Input Action controls how the Winch reacts to logic. You can use logic to simply turn it on and off, move it in one direction or the other, adjust its speed on the fly, and more. If you want it to pull really fast in one direction or the other, use the Flipper Type tweak. Use the Reversed tweak to swap what the Winch considers its beginning and ending motion. Use the Visible in Play Mode and Mute tweaks to determine whether a Winch can be seen or heard by your players! Finally, you may have noticed that the Winch has an output. This produces a signal value equivalent to the Winch’s progression through its movement cycle, so you can wire it up to whatever you like!

3168244169: An Advanced In/Out Mover is needed when you want precise control over which layers an object can move to and when it will move to them. Grab one out of the Gadgets page in your Tools Bag and let’s get right to it. First, place the Advanced In/Out Mover onto an object using the left stick and the action button, then open its tweak menu with the menu button.  Change the Maximum Speed tweak to determine how quickly the object will move between layers. With Allow Pushing set to No, the object’s movement will stop if it bumps into anything. If you set Allow Pushing to Yes, the object will instead shove any obstructions through the layers – even players! For more control over what it can and can’t push, you can change the Maximum Weight that Can Be Pushed.  Layer Boundaries determine which layers the object is allowed in. If the object is outside of its boundaries when you set them, or if you try to move it outside yourself, it will automatically snap back into its boundary, even without an input.  An Advanced In/Out Mover has two inputs. The first input can be set up to turn the mover on and off, affect the mover’s speed, or affect the mover’s strength. Attach logic to the second input to control its directional speed or to precisely determine the object’s position between its two boundaries! Finally, if your logic needs to know where an Advanced In/Out Mover is, consider using its output, which will send signals based on its location. Give it a shot!

3147142665: The Sackpocket Tweaker is used to give players items or take them away. It’s on the Creatures & Characters page of your Tools Bag, so place one down and let’s get started. First you’ll need to give the Sackpocket Tweaker an input – otherwise it won’t function. For now let’s use a simple button.  Next, enter the Sackpocket Tweaker’s tweak menu using the popit cursor and the menu button. You’ll want to choose an item if you want anything to happen, of course! From here you can open the Sackpocket Items page and choose from any of the official powerups or the ones you’ve made yourself. Just pick one with the action button and you’ll be taken back to the tweak menu. Now to determine what the Sackpocket Tweaker will actually be doing! With the Action tweak, you can tell it to Add an item to your player’s sackpocket or Remove it instead. There are actually two ways to Add a powerup – one only places it in the sackpocket, and the other also automatically equips the player with the item. With the quantity tweak you can change how many copies of the item the Sackpocket Tweaker adds or takes away. You can even give them an infinite amount if you want! The Affected Players tweak allows you to decide who gets the item. It can be all the players or just the one who triggered the tweaker. Finally, with the New Item Bubble tweak, you can turn the fancy “new item” bubble effect on and off. That effect is just for show, so turning it off won’t change anything else. With the Sackpocket Tweaker you can always be sure that your players have the right items at the right time. Have fun!

4227713906: A Spring is a connection between two objects that will always try to bounce back to its base length. They’re on the Gameplay page of the Tools Bag, so navigate to them with the left stick and select them with the action button. To place a connector, use the left stick to move your popit cursor to the surface of an object or material until you see it highlighted, and then press the action button to place the base. Then move your popit cursor to another surface and press the action button to place the other end. Now your two surfaces are connected! To open the Spring’s tweak menu, hover over it with the popit cursor and press the menu button. Now you’re presented with a load of options for customizing the Spring however you like. Let’s take a look at them. First, you can shorten or lengthen the Spring’s base length using the Length tweak. Just change the number with the left and right directional buttons or the left stick. Next, we have the Stiff tweak. Set it to Yes, and the Spring will stay rigid. Set it to No, and the Spring will flop around! The Strength tweak changes how hard the Spring tries to bounce back to its base length. Keep it high and the Spring will snap back into place with forceful speed; make it low and it’ll lazily slide back into place as long as it’s not met with any resistance.  Finally, use the Visible in Play Mode and Mute tweaks to determine whether a Spring can be seen or heard by your players!

2254091507: The Global Lighting Tweaker is used to change your level’s lighting settings on the fly. You can find it on the Gadgets page of your Tools Bag, so fetch one now and place it in a nice dark level. By default, a Global Lighting Tweaker is triggered by player proximity, so just walk up to it and watch as the lights come on! Obviously you can customize the lighting however you like, so let’s open the tweak menu with the popit cursor and the menu button. With the Lighting tweak, you can adjust the lighting from daylight to night time. Increase the Darkness tweak to give the level a nice shadowy feel. Increase the Fogginess to give your level a little haze. You can change the color of the fog, too! If you really want to go mad, try out some of the color correction options. If your Global Lighting Tweaker is being triggered by player proximity, you can increase or decrease the size of the trigger radius. Activate the Only Activate Once tweak if you want the lighting to change once, and then never again. Change the Transition Time to change how long it takes to change from the current lighting to the new lighting once the Global Lighting Tweaker has been triggered. Finally, it’s worth noting that you can also trigger the Global Lighting Tweaker via logic. Just wire a button or whatever else into its input!

4281519516: It’s time to learn about some shortcuts that will improve any level-building experience. First, let’s try Hiding. When something is in your way, but you don’t want to go to the trouble of moving it, you can make it invisible instead! Just point at the offending object with the Popit Cursor and press the L2 button. Now you can edit behind it as you please. You can even hide multiple objects at once for the really crowded bits. Once you’re done, be sure to Unhide everything with the L1 button! Next, let’s learn some ways to handle multiple objects simultaneously. First we have Drag Selecting, which allows you to pick up a big pile of stuff all at once. With your popit cursor out, hold down the action button and use the left stick to draw a box around the stuff you want to snag. When you’re done, just let go of the action button. Everything that was in the box will now be selected for you to move around, copy, flip, or anything else. Once you’re done, just press the back button. Finally, there’s Multiple Selecting. Like Drag Selecting, Multiple Select allows you to pick up multiple things at once. However, it’s a little more precise than Drag Selecting, so you should use this when you want to pick a few things out of a jumble. Just press and hold down the R2 button, then pick out whatever you like with the popit cursor and the action button. If you select something by mistake, just press the action button again. When you’ve selected everything you need, just let go of the R2 button to snatch everything up!

2373041914: A wobble bolt is just the thing for making stuff weave back and forth. Let’s get right to it. First, you’ll need something to bolt and something to bolt it to. Once you’ve sorted that out, find the wobble bolt in your tools bag. Position the bolt however you like using the left stick, then place it with the action button. Then move the bolted object in front of a nice sturdy base and attach it – again with the action button. The object will start wobbling right away. Now let’s tweak the wobble bolt. Open its tweak menu with the menu button. The first thing you’ll notice is the Rotation tweak, which determines how far your object rotates between wobbles. You can have anything from a gentle sway to a wild multi-rotation twister. Next, check out the Angle tweak. Changing this changes the base angle of the bolt’s rotation, so you can reorient the object without removing and reattaching the bolt.  The Time tweak determines the duration of each wobble. The Pause tweak determines how long the object waits between wobbles. The Sync tweak allows you to change when the wobble begins and ends relative to the rest of the timing in your level. The Strength tweak controls the force behind each wobble. The lower it is, the more the bolt is affected by outside forces.  The Input Action determines how a wobble bolt behaves when it receives a logic input, from simply turning on and off to precisely angling itself to match a positional value. If you want the wobble bolt to fling itself quickly in one direction or the other, use the Flipper Type tweak. Use the Reversed tweak to swap where the wobbling begins and ends. The visuals tweak determines whether the wobble bolt can be seen while your level is being played, and the Mute tweak determines whether it makes any noise.  Finally, a wobble bolt’s output produces a signal relative to its progression through its wobble cycle.

2156247009: If you have an idea for a level that will require some extra room, Dynamic Thermometer Levels are the answer. A Dynamic Thermometer Level allows you to stretch far beyond the usual space limitations, but there are some things to keep in mind to keep things running smoothly. Take a look now in your Global Stuff. You can change a level into a Dynamic Thermometer Level from the Gameplay Controls page; just tweak Dynamic Thermometer Level to yes. Immediately, you’ll notice that you have loads more space to build your level in!  A Dynamic Thermometer Level works by only loading certain parts of your level at a time. Every Dynamic Thermometer Level has a Loading Zone, which is an invisible box that follows the players throughout the level. Once a piece of your level is in the Loading Zone, it will load in and your players can see and interact with it. When a piece of the level isn’t in the Loading Zone anymore, it will load out, removing it from the level until it’s needed again. You can change the shape of the Loading Zone in the Dynamic Thermometer Level tweaks. This will help ensure your level is loading in the right pieces at the right time. If your level is very wide, for example, a wide Loading Zone will load pieces to the left and right of your players without worrying too much about what’s above and below them. This will make your level run more smoothly.  Similarly, you can also change the Loading Zone’s size. If your level is tightly packed full of complex workings, a smaller Loading Zone will make sure your level isn’t trying to load too much at once. But if your level has a lot of wide open spaces, a larger Loading Zone will prevent players from getting to areas before they load in. It’s important to realize that even if something is outside the Loading Zone, it will remain loaded in if it’s attached to something inside the Loading Zone. Keep your Dynamic Thermometer Levels organized into separate chunks to keep them running nicely. There are other tools to assist in keeping your Dynamic Thermometer Levels working correctly, too, but we’ll get to those in other tutorials.

2363472812: The Direction Combiner is used to take two different inputs and combine them into one output. Grab one from the Gadgets page of your Tools Bag, place it in the world, and hook it up to a Counter so we can see what it can do. Attach two separate buttons to each of the Direction Combiner’s positive and negative inputs, then jump around on them like a madman. Notice that as you push the positive button, the Counter goes up, and as you push the negative button, the Counter goes down! All from one input. Amazing stuff.  Now open up the Direction Combiner’s tweak menu using the menu button. You can invert its output – now when you push the buttons, they’re reversed! Finally, you can change the Output Value. The Combine Inputs tweak is a Direction Combiner as usual. The Angle-ify Inputs option is typically used with Controlinators and a control stick to combine both of the stick’s outputs into one angular value.

480847269: The Randomizer cycles through its outputs in an unpredictable pattern. Find one on the Gadgets page of your Tools Bag and place it in the world using the action button. To observe how the Randomizer behaves, hook up its output to a pack of lights. Notice that it turns them on and off one at a time, in no particular order. Naturally, this behavior can be altered via the tweak menu. Open it up using the menu button. The first tweak you’ll see is the Pattern tweak. The One at a Time pattern is the default. It turns on one output, then turns it off, then turns on another output. If you want to make sure it doesn’t pick the same output twice in a row, use the New pick each time tweak.  The Add pattern activates each output one by one without turning them off again. The Add and Reset When Full pattern does the same thing, but starts over again once it’s done. Lastly, the Toggle pattern randomly picks an output one at a time and reverses it – if it’s on, it turns off, and if it’s off, it turns on.  The Input Action changes how the Randomizer reacts to logic. You can use logic to simply turn the Randomizer on and off, or you can use logic signals to advance the Randomizer step by step. In the on time category, you can set up a minimum and maximum time for the Randomizer to leave its outputs activated. These times can be identical if you like, but if they’re different the Randomizer will randomly choose durations between the two numbers. The off time category is the same, except it controls how long the outputs stay deactivated. Finally, to reverse the Randomizer's behavior, activate the Invert Output tweak. Now it leaves its outputs on and turns them off randomly instead!

878579066: As part of your Play, Create, and Share experience, sharing your newly created levels couldn't be simpler. First, go to your Moon and highlight the level you wish to publish with left stick. Then, press the menu button to bring up the level’s More Page. Once it’s up, you can move the left stick to highlight the level name option. Press the action button to give your level a snazzy name or something as plain as Jane. Just make sure you pick something nice. Next, use the left stick to select the level badge option and press the action button. You can choose any stickers you've collected or created to help visually represent your level to the rest of the Imagisphere. Once you’re done with that, use the left stick to scroll down to the labels options. Once you’ve selected it with the action button, choose from a multitude of labels that quickly describe what kind of level you've created. You can select up to five labels at a time using the action button, so make sure you choose wisely. And if you need to be a bit more descriptive, select the level description option with the action button to let people know what it’s about and how you got the idea, and then some. There are even more options you can add to your level as well: if you set it to be locked only players who have its level key can play it. If you are feeling generous, you can let other Sack persons copy your masterpiece to their moons if you set it to be copyable. You can even make it a sub-level where your level is invisible to other players and can only be accessed by a level link. Once you’re done, just select publish with the action button and you'll be sent to your Earth where you can use the left stick to position it anywhere you feel is perfect for your masterpiece. Slap it down with the action button and your amazing new creation is now a part of LittleBigPlanet history!

1553884763: A String is a connection between two objects that has a maximum length, but otherwise allows the two objects to fly and flop around as much as you want them to. They’re on the Gameplay page of the Tools Bag, so navigate to them with the left stick and select them with the action button. To place a connector, use the left stick to move your popit cursor to the surface of an object or material until you see it highlighted, and then press the action button to place the base. Then move your popit cursor to another surface and press the action button to place the other end. Now your two surfaces are connected! To open the String’s tweak menu, hover over it with the popit cursor and press the menu button. The String is pretty simple, so it shouldn’t take long to figure them out.  First of all, you can shorten or lengthen the String’s length using the Length tweak. Just change the number with the left and right directional buttons or the left stick. And lastly, use the Visible in Play Mode and Mute tweaks to determine whether a String can be seen or heard by your players!

2630918292: An AND gate outputs a signal only when all of its inputs are active. Find one on the Gadgets page of your Tools Bag, and then use the left stick and action button to select it and place it onto a Microchip.  Attach a switch to each of the AND gate’s inputs. Notice that if you activate the switches one at a time, the AND gate will do nothing. However, if you activate both switches at once, the AND gate will light up and produce a signal! That’s an AND gate at its very simplest. Now hover your popit cursor over the AND gate and press the menu button to open its tweak menu. From here, you can add more ports in order to make the AND gate require more inputs using the Number of Ports tweak. With the Invert Output tweak you can reverse the AND Gate’s output so that it only turns off once it receives all its inputs.  Finally, use the Output Value tweak to change whether the AND Gate produces a signal based on its lowest input or whether its signal is based on all its inputs multiplied together. Note that this is a fairly advanced option and doesn’t need to be touched for basic use!

1103461805: Creatures are a simple way of filling your levels with enemies. Once you’ve made a body, you’ll find everything you need to bring it to life in your Tools Bag. First, your creature needs a brain or two. Place some on your creature using the left stick and the action button. There are two types of brain: protected and unprotected. They both function in exactly the same way, with one very important difference. Sackthings can destroy unprotected brains by touching them, but protected brains can only be destroyed by logic. A creature can have multiple brains on it, and once they’re all destroyed, the creature is killed.  Next, your creature probably needs a way to move around. For this, we have Legs and Wheels. Place them on your creature just like a brain, and your creature will take off running! You can give your creature some personality by adding eyes. You can even tweak their colors! These are just for show, though. To really change how a creature acts, you’ll want to turn back to their brains. Let’s tweak one now. First, notice the behavior tweak. This determines how the creature reacts to players. If you leave it on Ignore, the creature will go on its merry way, not paying any attention to your players. Setting it to Follow means the creature will chase after them; setting it to Flee makes your creature a scaredy-cat who runs away from them instead. Make the creature’s Awareness Radius bigger or smaller to determine when it notices players and reacts to them. You can attach logic to creature brains! Tweak its Input Action to change whether logic turns the creatures on and off or kills them. On to vulnerability. Make a creature vulnerable to lethal materials if you want it to get killed if it stumbles into hazards. Otherwise it can go anywhere it pleases. Change the creature’s destroy effect to change its death anything from simply vanishing to a fantastically messy splat. And finally, movement. Tweak a creature’s movement speed to make it scamper around faster or slower. Tweak its jumping strength to change how high it can jump, tweak its jump interval to change how often it jumps, and tweak its jump phase to change when it starts jumping. To make sure your creatures stay where they belong, place Creature Navigators to give their movement boundaries. Just make sure they can’t jump over them! Now you can litter your levels with life!

492526841: Transporting one’s self from the Earthly plateaux to the realm of LittleBigPlanet™ is akin to being born again. You emerge here a bundle of naked woolly innocence. The operative word being ‘naked.’ Put some clothes on that say ‘I mean business, buster.’ Get some gad-about-trousers or an adventurer’s hat for example.  To do so, bring up your POPIT with the MENU BUTTON and select the CUSTOMIZE CHARACTER OPTION. From there you can peruse its contents with the LEFT STICK and don your chosen attire with the ACTION BUTTON. Once you are suitably suited and booted having raided your boutique, a press of the BACK BUTTON shows off your new togs to your peers. If you live by the sea that is.

320361150: The Global Visual Options determine the appearance and lighting of your level. You can find them on the Global Controls page of your Global Stuff, so head there now and take a look! Change the Lighting tweak to determine your level’s time of day. Increase the Darkness tweak to fill your level with spooky shade! Use the Fogginess tweak to adjust the fog levels in your level, and the Fog Color tweak to change what color it is. In the Color Correction tweak, there’s a pack of crazy options for making your level look especially weird. Choose a Background for your level with the Backgrounds menu. Just highlight one that looks good and press the action button. Once you’ve done that, you can adjust its position with the next few tweaks! This is only for show, so make sure it looks right alongside the rest of your level. If you don’t want a Background at all, you can turn it off instead! Finally, you can change the behavior of the camera in your level. The Standard Zoom tweak controls how close or far away the camera is in your level. The Maximum Zoom tweak controls how far your camera can zoom out when your players are all spread out. With the depth of field options, you can adjust your shot’s depth of field and its flatness, and whether this changes relative to players!

1630546348: The Corner Editor is used to reshape the corners of your materials. You can find it on the Tools page of your Tools Bag, so select it now.  With the Corner Editor selected, move the cursor over a material using the left stick, then select it using the action button. Notice that the selected material’s corners are highlighted as you move the cursor near them. You can select them with the action button and drag them around with the left stick! Once you’ve moved the corner where you want it, just press the action button to set it, then press the back button to back out of corner editing altogether. You can add a new corner to a selected material by simply moving the cursor between two existing corners and pressing the action button. You can delete any corner by selecting it and pressing the delete button. Finally, if you want to select multiple corners at once, select a material, then press and hold the action button and use the left stick to drag a box around each corner you want to select. Let go of the action button and you’ll have them all selected at once, to move around or delete as you please!

3198284612: A XOR Gate produces a signal when one of its inputs, and only one of its inputs, is active. Find one on the Gadgets page of your Tools Bag, and then use the left stick and action button to select it and place it onto a Microchip.  Attach a switch to each of the XOR Gate’s inputs. Notice that when you activate one switch, the XOR Gate lights up and produces a signal, but when you activate the other one, the XOR Gate shuts down. Now hover your popit cursor over the XOR Gate and press the menu button to open its tweak menu. From here, you can add more ports using the Number of Ports tweak. However, the XOR Gate only produces a signal when it has a single input, no matter how many ports it has! Finally, use the Invert Output tweak to reverse the XOR Gate’s signal – it will only turn off when it has a single input!

530731102: The Popit Powerup allows you to give players Create tools in Play mode! Perfect for creating your own Popit Puzzles or whatever other crazy ideas you might think up. Like other powerups, it’s found in the Creatures & Characters page of your Tools Bag. The Popit Powerup has lots of tweaks, so dive right in with the menu button.  In the Inventory category you can select which goodies and tools your players have access to in their popit. Just open each menu and scroll to whichever item you like, then highlight it with the action button. You can highlight as many objects and tools as you like. Your player will have access to all of them. Use the Popit Cursor tweak to enable or disable the popit cursor. Use the VCR Controls tweak to enable or disable things like Undo and Pause. If these are enabled, you can also use the Freeze Sackboy When Paused tweak to prevent players from running around while time is stopped! With the Grid Snap tweak, choose between any of the three grid sizes or no grid at all. Set the Layer Boundaries to restrict the player’s popit use to certain layers. Finally, if the player will need the Popit Powerup throughout your whole level, you may as well prevent them from dropping it by using the Can Be Dropped tweak.

1233721476: Elastic is a rubbery connection between two objects that will try to snap back to its base length. They’re on the Gameplay page of the Tools Bag, so navigate to them with the left stick and select them with the action button. To place a connector, use the left stick to move your popit cursor to the surface of an object or material until you see it highlighted, and then press the action button to place the base. Then move your popit cursor to another surface and press the action button to place the other end. Now your two surfaces are connected! To open the Elastic’s tweak menu, hover over it with the popit cursor and press the menu button. Now you’re presented with a set of options for customizing the Elastic however you like. Let’s take a peek. First, you can shorten or lengthen the Elastic’s base length using the Length tweak. Just change the number with the left and right directional buttons or the left stick. Next, the Elastic’s Strength determines how hard it snaps back to its original length when it gets stretched out. Set it high and it’ll be quick like a slingshot! Set it low and it’ll barely bother at all.  Finally, use the Visible in Play Mode and Mute tweaks to determine whether Elastic can be seen or heard by your players!

515657177: Sticker panel is a special material with a few unique properties that make it very useful for level creators. Let’s put some down and have a go. The first thing to notice is that sticker panel has no collision, so things will pass right through it. That means it’s a handy place to store microchips, emitters, and other pieces of logic – sticker panel is easily portable and will never get in the way. You can make it invisible by tweaking its opacity. Your players won’t even know it’s there! That isn’t all it’s for, though. It’s called sticker panel for a reason! Watch what happens when you slap a sticker onto it. Voila! The sticker takes center stage. The surrounding material becomes invisible in play mode.  You can change the appearance of the sticker by tweaking the sticker panel. You can affect the sticker’s color, its brightness and its opacity!  Finally, notice that you can have two sets of colors, brightnesses, and opacities – just set up the sticker panel’s Color When Off options. You can change from one to the other using the sticker panel’s input. Just set the input action to on/off or, if you want a nice smooth transition, set it to dimmer. Sticker panel is the perfect material for filling your creations with stickery goodness. Learn to love it!

1036216695: Slides are a simple and fun way to get your players from the back layers to the front ones. Grab one from the Gameplay page of your Tools Bag and let’s give it a try. You can shape and position a slide just like any other material. Move it around with the left stick and resize it with the right stick. Move it in and out of layers with the left shoulder buttons, and make it longer or shorter with the right shoulder buttons. After you place it in the world with the action button, you can also customize the slide’s shape using the Corner Editor, just like with a normal material. Now open up the slide’s tweak menu using the tweak button. With the Choose Material tweak, you can customize the slide’s appearance. Just select an appropriate material for your level. If the material you choose is color tweakable, you can select its color down below. Use the Impact Damping tweak to determine whether players are met by friction upon hitting the slide, or whether they reach top speed right away. The Slide Speed tweak controls how fast players go once they get going, and the Steering tweak determines how much or how little control they have over their movement as they slide down. Finally, activate the Base tweak to give the Slides visible sides, but be warned that these are only visual, and players can walk right through them!

1114511251: Whether it’s part of a larger adventure or just a one-off, every level ends eventually. The scoreboard is the classic way to finish a level off. Take a look. Like most objects, the scoreboard can be static or dynamic. Let’s make sure it stays in place by setting this one to be static. Now on to the fun stuff: gifts! You can fill a scoreboard with three prize bubbles per category. The categories are as follows: First, the Level Complete Gifts. Everyone who finishes the level gets these. Second, the Aced Level Gifts. If a player beats your level without any gruesome hiccups, they’ll earn this lot. And lastly, the Collected All Gifts. These are for players who have found all the other prizes in your level. The Shareable tweak determines whether your players can give share prizes with other players. If you want them to be able to share, select Yes. If you want them to keep the prizes to themselves, select No. If you have nothing to give away, that’s fine. You don’t need to put any gifts into a scoreboard for it to function. The Level Link options control where your player winds up after they trigger the scoreboard. If your level’s a one-off, you can ignore this. Players will just wind up safe in their pods. But if you want them to move on to the next chapter in your soaring saga, just choose the relevant level from the list. If you’ve labeled multiple start points in the level, you can choose the right label from the list below the link. 3385299011: A sackbot is a customizable sackthing that will behave however you like.  You can find them on the Creatures & Characters page of your Tools Bag. Place one in the world using the left stick and the action button. There it is: alive and ready to learn. Let’s give it a tweak or two and tell it what to do. First let’s decide what it looks like. A sackbot can be shaped like any of LittleBigPlanet 3’s characters – Sackboy, Odd sock, Toggle, or Swoop. For now, let’s leave this one as Sackboy and give it a costume. A sackbot can have its own costume, or it can mimic one of the costumes your players are wearing. Let’s just give this one a hat. Changing a sackbot’s animation style changes which character it moves like. Just pick the one you think looks best! You can give it a silly head size, too, if you’re in the mood, and you can its facial expressions as well. A sackbot can be anywhere from mildly cheerful to soul-crushingly sad. It’s up to you! Now let’s make it move. Tweak its walking speed to make it move slower or faster. By default, a sackbot will just stand still, so tweak its behavior to make it follow players, run away from them, patrol back and forth, or chase after tags. For extra-precise control, you can use the Act behavior. This will give you direct control of the sackbot until you press the back button, and then save everything you did. With the record sound option, you can even make it talk! You can have it playback your actions once, or you can have it repeat them. The loop relative option will make it playback the actions no matter where it is; if you set it to loop absolute, it’ll try to get back to its original starting place first.  If your sackbot is reacting to players or tags, you can customize its awareness radius to be as large or small as you want. You can also give it specific behavior changes in the AI tweaks category: whether it can change layers, swim, or jump, and whether it’s right- or left-handed. A sackbot that is afraid of danger will avoid touching hazards like fire and plasma. A sackbot that is afraid of heights won’t jump into any holes it can’t jump out. Lastly, a sackbot set to be hostile will shove themselves into the players they’re following; a non-hostile one will stop a polite distance away. In the powerups category, you can tweak which powerups a sackbot can equip.  You can assign an actor name to a sackbot in order to link them to magic mouths and animation tweakers. The look at category determines what a sackbot pays attention to, and how quickly it moves its gaze. Note that if it’s looking at a target tag, that’s what it will shoot its powerups at as well.  A sackbot can now have two different forms! Set it to be a changeling and alternate between its two selves with the change button. Finally, a behavior chip allows you to trigger new behaviors for your sackbots via logic. They have most of the same options a sackbot does so you can swap behaviors on the fly!

3666510327: The Preloader is an advanced tool for managing your Dynamic Thermometer Levels. It allows you to use logic or player positioning to tell the game to load an area in your level that it wouldn’t otherwise be loading. It’s on the Tools page of your Tools Bag, so take one out and take a peek at its tweak menu. The Place Zone option lets you shape a box around the area of your level that the Preloader will load. Anything inside the box will be loaded in when the Preloader activates. Change it the same way you’d change a camera zone or an emitter zone, and once you’ve set it up, just press the action button.  Next check out the Load Type tweak. You have two options: Preload and Full Load. If the zone is Preloaded, it’s not quite in the game yet, but it’s in queue and ready to go once the players get there. This is helpful when you need the game to know where your players are going, but you don’t want it to devote all its resources to loading the area quite yet. Conversely, a Full Load does it all – the area is fully loaded right then and there! This can be useful, but always be mindful of not telling a Dynamic Thermometer Level to load too much at once. If your Preloader is going to be triggered by player proximity, set up the trigger zone in the Trigger category, and change whether it requires all players in the Behavior category. You can ignore these tweaks if your Preloader is triggered by logic instead. Finally, you may have noticed that the Preloader has an output. This will start giving a signal once the Preloader has loaded its designated area so that you can delay logic until the area is ready to go!

2926769090: The Springinator Sensor allows you to detect when a Spinginator-equipped OddSock bounces on any object. 971532203: The Camera Excluder material is a special material that tells game cameras to ignore any players who are touching it. You can find it on the Materials page of your Goodies Bag along with the rest of the materials, so grab some now and smear it down with the action button. Observe how the camera behaves when you touch the Camera Excluder. It stops tracking your movement until you exit the Camera Excluder space! This is great for keeping the camera from following players into deadly pits, secret rooms, and more.  You can shape the Camera Excluder and Corner Edit it just like any other material, and it’s totally invisible to players. You can even turn it on and off via its logic input!

3521417129: The Counter produces a signal after it receives a specific number of inputs. Grab one from the Gadgets page of your Tools Bag and use the left stick and the action button to put it in the world. Attach a button to the Counter’s increment input and push it a few times. See how the bar progressively fills up? By default, a Counter needs ten inputs before it activates. Push the button ten times and the output lights up, see? Now wire another button to the reset input and push that. The bar clears out!  Now use the popit cursor and the menu button to open up the Counter’s tweak menu. Adjust the Target Count tweak to determine how many signals the Counter needs before it activates. If you don’t want it to start its count from zero, you can adjust the Current Count tweak as well. Finally, you can invert the Counter’s output so that it turns off after a certain number of inputs instead!

2316817547: Take a look at the Force Chip, which flings nearby objects and characters away from itself. It’s on the Gadgets page of your Tools Bag.  The first thing you’ll notice when you set one down is that without an input, a Force Chip will constantly shove things away! You probably want to attach an input to it. So for now we’ll just use a simple button.  Enter the Force Chip’s tweak menu with the menu button. The first tweak you’ll notice is the Strength tweak, which controls how strong the Force Chip pushes. You can even give it a negative Strength to make it attract things instead! To enlarge or shrink the range of the Force Chip’s effect, tweak the Range and Layer Detection Range tweaks.  Finally, you can control what the Force Chip can push around. The Affect Sack Things tweak changes whether characters are affected. If you’d rather it only affected objects with a certain tag, use the Tagged Objects tweak. You can also set it up to ignore certain tags. With what you’ve learned here, you’ll be forcing stuff around in no time!

1122771480: The Gyroscope does all it can to orient the object it’s on in a single direction. Grab one from the Gadgets page of your Tools Bag and place it onto an object with the action button. The direction your Gyroscope is pointing determines the direction it will rotate its object. Select the Gyroscope and use the right stick to point it in whatever direction you like, then watch as the object reacts!  Now use the popit cursor and the menu button to open the Gyroscope’s tweak menu. The Rotation Speed tweak determines how fast the Gyroscope orients its object, and the Direction of Rotation tweak changes whether the Gyroscope rotates clockwise, anti-clockwise, or both. The Acceleration tweak determines how hard the Gyroscope tries to orient its object in the correct direction. Finally, the Input Action tweak changes how the Gyroscope reacts to logic. You can simply turn it on and off, or adjust its speed or strength on the fly!

3957885035: The Controlinator is a powerful tool that outputs logic signals based on your controller's actions! You can find it on the Gadgets page of your Tools Bag. Select it and place it in the world with the action button.  Notice that if you jump in and fiddle with buttons on your controller, the corresponding outputs on the Controlinator will start lighting up! You may have also noticed the output in the middle of the Controlinator light up. This gives a signal when a Controlinator is occupied by a Sackthing, so you’ll be able to tell when your Controlinators are being used. There are also outputs that react to your controller’s orientation in the real world! Use these for levels with motion control! You can exit the Controlinator in Create by pushing in the right stick.  Let’s take a look at its tweak menu with the popit cursor and the menu button. You can give your Controlinator a name if you like; this is just for organization’s sake. Helpful for a level with lots of Controlinators!  Next, determine whether your Controlinator has remote control functionality. A transmitter will send its outputs to any receivers of the same color. For example, if you have a pack of Sackbots with red receivers on them, a player in a red transmitter can control all of them simultaneously! Also worth noting is the Controlled by Nearest Player option on receivers. With this selected, your player can control a Controlinator without actually needing to be inside of it. If you don’t want a player using your Controlinator to have access to their Popit, activate the Disable Popit Controls tweak. Use the Set Trigger Radius and Layer Range tweaks to determine how close a Sackthing needs to be to enter the Controlinator. Activate the Automatically Enter tweak and they’ll be forced into the Controlinator as soon as they come in range. Change the Players tweak if you only want your lead player to be able to use the Controlinator. The tweaks in the display category determine how the Controlinator appears for you in Create. You can open and close the circuitboard and, if your Controlinator is at an odd angle, you can stabilize it as well. Finally, the visuals category. If your Controlinator has a mess of wires coming out of it and you’d rather not see them, activate the Hide Outgoing Wires when Circuitboard is Closed tweak. The side-mounted tweak changes how Sackthings appear whilst inside the Controlinator. And, as always, you can tweak its visibility in play mode.

1394423376: The Slice ‘N Dice tool allows you to carve up your materials into separate shapes. You can find it on the Tools page of your Tools Bag, so take it out and let’s carve some stuff! With the Slice ‘N Dice tool selected, use the left stick to navigate the cursor to the material you want to affect. Highlight it by hovering over it and press the action button to select it. If you change your mind, you can deselect the material with the back button. Move your cursor to one of the selected material’s edges and press the action button. Move the left stick again and you’ll see a line stretching from the edge to your cursor – this is the line the Slice ‘N Dice tool will carve. Just stretch the line from one edge to another and press the action button to make your cut. If you want a more complicated cut, you can press the action button mid-shape to make a corner and start a new line. Just be sure to finish by pressing the action button on an edge. You can even end on the same edge you started on if you want! When you’re done carving, deselect the shape with the back button. Now the material is split into two pieces that are glued together. 2008552059: When you need crazy movement in every direction through multiple layers, the Bendy Rails are the way to go. Find them on the Gameplay page of your Tools Bag and give them a shot. Use the left stick and the shuffle buttons to position the first end of your Bendy Rail. You can attach the Bendy Rails to materials and objects in your level, but unlike other connectors, Bendy Rails can also be free-floating, so you can put them wherever you want. Once you’ve decided where to place it, press the action button. Use the left stick, shuffle buttons, and action button to place the next node of your Bendy Rail… and the next… and the next. Observe how the Bendy Rail previews its bends and curves as you set up its nodes. Use this to set it up just how you like. Once you’re finished, press the back button to complete your Bendy Rail or just attach another end to an object to complete it automatically. Now it’s time to tweak your Bendy Rail. Place your popit cursor over it and press the menu button. The Interacts With tweak changes what can attach to your Bendy Rail. You can choose between sackthings on Hook Hats, Rail Hooks, both, or – if your Bendy Rail is just for show – nothing at all. Use the Choose Material tweak to decide what your Bendy Rail is made of. You can even customize its color if you select a color tweakable material. If you’d rather your Bendy Rail weren’t visible at all, you can do that, too. Finally, if you want to change the shape of your Bendy Rail after you’ve placed it, you’ll need to use the Rail Editor tool. It’s on the Tools page. To use it, position it over your Bendy Rail with the left stick and press the action button. The ends and nodes of the Bendy Rail will be highlighted. You can select the nodes with the action button and move them about as normal, or delete them with the delete button. If you move the cursor between two nodes, you can even add a new node using the action button. Now you’re ready for your levels to go in, out, and all around!

879317699: When you need to give your players a powerup, why not try the Powerup Pedestals? There are two kinds, and you can find both on the Creatures & Characters page of your Tools Bag. Snatch up one of each and we’ll learn them both. The Powerup Pedestal is for powerups your players don’t get to keep. Open up its tweak menu with the menu button and select the Choose Adventure Item option. From here, you’ll find the Sackpocket Items page, where you can choose from the readymade powerups like the Pumpinator, or whatever crazy contraptions you’ve devised yourself in the My Sackpocket Items category. You can even capture a new powerup using the Capture Sackpocket Item option! Once you’ve chosen your desired item, just highlight it and press the action button. The Can Be Dropped tweak controls whether players can unequip the powerup manually. The other pedestal is the Sackpocket Pedestal, which is used to place powerups in your players’ Sackpocket! It works pretty much the same way – just select an item from the Sackpocket Items page and you’re good to go. You can even toggle the New Item Bubble tweak if you’re feeling really fancy! This will display the powerup in a flashy bubble once it’s collected. It’s just for show!

2345395121: The Weather Materials are special materials you can use to fill your levels with amazing visual effects. Let’s take a look at them now. You can find them with the rest of the materials in your Goodies Bag, so highlight the basic Weather Material and use the action button to select it and place it in the world. Right away, the rain begins to fall! Note that this effect is just for show. Characters and objects are able to pass right through the Weather Material. If you want to customise the weather particles, open up the Weather Material’s tweak menu with the menu button. Select any colour you like for your weather particles. You can also adjust the colour brightness or the overall opacity. To make the particles fall faster or slower, tweak their animation speed. You can even make them fall backwards by selecting a negative speed! To change which kind of particles you’re seeing, use the Atmospheric Type tweak. The Atmospheric Intensity tweak changes how many particles you see at once. If you’re using snow, you can vary the path the particles take by adjusting the Direction Strength. Like most other colour tweakable materials, you can have two sets of colours – just set up the Weather Material’s Colour When Off options. Things like opacity and animation speed can be changed as well, so be sure to examine each option! You can change from one state to the other using the Weather Material’s input. Just set the input action to on/off or, if you want a nice smooth transition, set it to dimmer. Finally, don’t forget the other Weather Material: the Sticker Weather Material. This shares most tweaks with the normal Weather Material, but you can replace the weather particles with any sticker you like. Want your level to rain fish or snow socks? Go right ahead!

4125532070: In Dynamic Thermometer Levels, there are two types of loading zones. First, there’s the loading zone around the player. Second, there’s the loading zones created by the objects and logic in the level. Dynamic Thermometer Levels work by following this simple rule: when the player’s loading zone intersects with the loading zone of an object, the object gets loaded in! It’s important to know when and how loading zones get created and what determines their shape and size. Let’s show you how the shapes and sizes of object loading zones are determined and how this affects your Dynamic Thermometer. Every object in your level has its own invisible loading zone in the shape of a rectangular box around it. When you connect multiple objects together by gluing, they will be considered one object and share a loading zone in the form of a square box around all the glued objects. A similar thing happens when you connect two objects together using a connector...or a logic wire. Sensors that have a radius also affect the size and shape of the loading zone they belong to. The loading zone will be a rectangle around the maximum radius. Additionally, you can create your own loading zone around multiple objects by using the loading linker tool. Simply select the Loading Linker from Dynamic Thermometer section the Tools Bag and tap the Action Button on multiple objects to group them together in a loading zone. When you are finished selecting the objects, press the cancel button to create your new loading zone. If you want an object to be permanently loaded in, you can use the Permanency Tweaker tool. To use the Permanency Tweaker, grab one from the Dynamic Thermometer section your Tools Bag and place it on an object. That object and all objects in the same loading zone will now always be loaded in!
