3600399117: A Note is primarily used in Create mode to label and keep track of your most complicated creations!  But now, you can use it to add lots of eye popping text in your levels!  Grab one from the Gadgets page of your Tools Bag and let’s see how it works. Open the Note’s tweak menu with the menu button. Let’s start by using the Note tweak to write a message for your Note to store!  As you can see, the text pops up right away. You can show or hide the text with the Show tweak… or you can select it with the popit cursor and press the grab button.  We can also change the font type and font size as well! Select the Font Type tweak and cycle through the different types with the Left Stick until you find one you like. Next, select the Text Size tweak and use the Left Stick to change the size of the font. You can make it as small or as big as you want it to be. You can also change the Text Colour and Background Colour of your note! Just like other colour changeable objects, select the colour you want your font and background to be by selecting a colour in the colour palette.  You can also change the brightness of the colour as well using the Text Brightness and Background Brightness options.  You can also change the Opacity of the background if you want your font to pop out even more or have no background at all! In the Visuals settings, you can set the note to have No visibility in Play Mode, Text Only, or have the Note and Text be visible.  If the Local Space setting is set to No, your text will always be upright regardless of the note’s orientation.  If it’s set to Yes, the text will be aligned with the note’s orientation like so. With Input Action, you can set what happens with a note when you place an output into its input.  Using Open simply brings up the text you have inputted when it receives a 100% signal and closes when it does not. When using signal strength, you can visibly see the signal strength of any output you connect to the note. Make sure you change the number format options below to see the measurements properly. Tweaking Max Value changes the total value that is represented at 100% signal strength. Tweaking Decimals changes how many decimals are shown in your value. Finally, you can also add a Suffix to your text if you wanted to add an identifier to your signal strength value such as weight, speed, or even the total number of cupcakes!

4066876657: If the animations on an object need changing, it’s time to bring out an Object Animation Tweaker. They’re found on the Creatures & Characters page of your Tools Bag, so grab one now and slap it on an animated object. Right away, you’ll notice a change: the animation stops! You can have it start and end at any point in the animation’s usual cycle. Be sure your tweaks are having the desired effect – it’s really easy to make things look very strange! With the Reset if Inactive tweak set to Yes, the animation will start over from the beginning whenever it’s triggered. If you set it to No, then it will start from wherever it left off – even if that means the very last frame. Change the Input Action to make the Object Animation Tweaker react differently to logic. You can turn it on and off, make it play slower or faster, and other such changes. Try them out! Finally, observe the sequencer bar that progresses as the animation plays. Using this, you can trigger logic based on animation timing!

678119220: The Sound Object is the way to fill your levels with noise! You can find it on the Music page of your Tools Bag. Put one in the world with the action button and let’s have a go! By default, a Sound Object is triggered by player proximity. Just wander over to it a few times to hear it go off! Naturally, there are lots of tweaks and noises to choose from. Open up the Sound Object’s tweak menu using the menu button. First, open up the Choose Sound option with the action button. From here, you can choose a sound category on the left side of the menu. Scroll through the categories to see their available noises on the right! You may notice that some noises have asterisks by their names. This signifies that the noise is a nice steady perpetual noise rather than a one-off. Once you see a noise you like, just select it with the action button and back out of the menu with the back button. The Trigger Mode tweak determines when the sound plays. It can be played when the player is nearby, when things bump into the object it’s on, or when the object it’s on is created or destroyed! You can also use logic to trigger a Sound Object. If you do, you can change how it reacts to an input with the Input Action tweak. The Volume tweak controls how loud the noise is, and the Sound Modifier tweak lets you play it at higher or lower pitches. Activate the Position Sound tweak if you want the sound to play based on its location in the world, or keep it off if you just want the sound to play at full volume no matter where it is! Finally, you may have noticed that the Sound Object has another input. You can use this to adjust the sound’s pitch on the fly using logic!

3719081071: When you’re working in a Dynamic Thermometer Level, there will sometimes be occasions when you want to be sure two things will always load in at the same time. For example, if you have a platform for Sackbots to walk on, but the Sackbots load before the platform, they’ll just fall into space! If you seem to be having issues like this, the Loading Linker will sort it right out. It’s on the Tools page of your Tools Bag. While in a Dynamic Thermometer Level, just select the Loading Linker. Notice how everything on screen becomes outlined in a certain color? Everything of a certain color is in the same loading group. Things in the same loading group will always load in together. To place two things into the same loading group, just hover the Loading Linker over one object and press the action button, then do the same with the second object. See, now they’re the same color. It’s as simple as that. Just be sure you don’t link too many things together to ensure your level runs properly!

3075588698: A Piston is a rod-like connection between two objects that can get longer and shorter. They’re on the Gameplay page of the Tools Bag, so navigate to them with the left stick and select them with the action button. To place a connector, use the left stick to move your popit cursor to the surface of an object or material until you see it highlighted, and then press the action button to place the base. Then move your popit cursor to another surface and press the action button to place the other end. Now your two surfaces are connected! Notice how the Piston contracts and expands, moving the lower object up and down. Also observe that the Piston is stiff! There’s no interrupting this motion.  Let’s tweak the Piston by moving the popit cursor over it and pressing the menu button. The first tweak you’ll see is the Maximum Length tweak, which controls how long the Piston can get. Similarly, the Minimum Length tweak sets up the Piston when it’s at its shortest. If you don’t want the Piston to be stiff, you can turn off the Stiff tweak. Now you can shove it around a bit, but it can still shove back! Adjust the Time tweak to change how long it takes for the Piston to stretch from its minimum to its maximum length and back. If you want it to pause for a while at each end, use the Pause tweak. To sync its timing relative to the rest of the timing in your level, use the Sync tweak! The Strength tweak controls how hard the Piston tries to push and pull when it’s met with resistance. At 0% it won’t even move at all. What a slacker! The Input Action controls how the Piston reacts to logic. You can use logic to simply turn it on and off, move it in one direction or the other, adjust its speed on the fly, and more. If you want it to pull really fast in one direction or the other, use the Flipper Type tweak. Use the Reversed tweak to swap what the Piston considers its beginning and ending motion. Use the Visible in Play Mode and Mute tweaks to determine whether a Piston can be seen or heard by your players! Finally, you may have noticed that the Piston has an output. This produces a signal value equivalent to the Piston’s progression through its movement cycle, so you can wire it up to whatever you like!

2596793545: The Blaster Handle is used to create custom powerups for your levels and adventures! Select an appropriate object for your powerup, and then put a Blaster Handle on it from the Creatures & Characters page of your Tools Bag. Note that a Sackthing will grip the object from the spot you place the Blaster Handle on, so place it carefully. With the Blaster Handle placed, go to the Sackpocket Items page of your Global Stuff, then capture the object. The object will be added to the My Sackpocket Items category and can be equipped!  Of course, it doesn’t actually do anything yet. That’s fine! Now that it’s on the Sackpocket Items page, you can open its menu with the menu button and select Recapture to update it to your latest version.  Let’s make some changes now. On the original object, open the Blaster Handle’s tweak menu. The first tweak is the Grip tweak. Use this to determine how your Sackthing holds the powerup: with a fist or with an open palm! This is purely a visual tweak, so just pick what works! Change the Aiming Speed tweak to adjust how quickly the powerup moves around in a Sackthing’s hand.  If the Allow Grabbing/Climbing tweak is disabled, the powerup will prevent a player from grabbing or climbing until they unequip it. Now you’ve probably noticed that the Blaster Handle has a circuit board like a microchip’s. This is where the real fun begins! Here you can put any logic you like to make the powerup – or its owner –do incredible things. Try it out and go crazy! One special thing to note is the Trigger output. This produces a signal whenever the powerup’s owner presses the grab button, so you can easily make simple one-button powerups!

2979908434: Aha, you have one of those deliciously tactile PlayStation®Vita systems I see.  It’s like holding a little piece of hardware-heaven isn’t it. Delectation for y’digits.  And connected to your PlayStation®3 system too!? You’re a whiz, and you can cover me in wool and call me Sackboy if it aint so!  As before your best chum is y’Popit, so let’s meet it shall we. Open the Popit menu by pressing the POPIT BUTTON … and select the Goodies Bag.  We’re going to draw some material into the level … … and have a faff around with it so use your LEFT STICK and ACTION BUTTON to do so.  Or, use the fabulous TOUCHSCREEN facility, it’s your lifestyle choice.  You select objects by placing the Popit Cursor over them and pressing the … … ACTION BUTTON, … or by touching it using the TOUCHSCREEN.  Once selected, press and hold the L BUTTON.  Your keen eye will have no doubt spotted the panel that comes up on the right side of the TOUCHSCREEN.  This enables you to alter which layer it’s in by moving the LEFT STICK up and down and … you can change it from thin to thick by moving the RIGHT STICK up and down.  If wiggling sticks isn’t your thing then… you can also use your finger to move it from back to front and thick to thin.  Ah the wonder of your TOUCHSCREEN. It’s literally incandescent with interactivity. Try it. Slide your favorite finger across the screen and see how the Popit cursor instantly falls in love with you … and follows your every move.  This magic also works on objects within the game. They too form an instant attraction to you and obey your every deft finger swish. You can select things from your Popit menu via the gift of touch too. Amazing, but that’s just the start of it.  A PlayStation®Vita system has ultra modern sensors front and back, … making it practically sentient.  Use the REAR TOUCH PAD to, for example, move the camera around. One finger can pan the camera whilst another two of your digits control the zoom in and out. Of course, our old friend the Right Stick is there too to do the same job if you want.  Mustn’t forget old Righty.  You could dive in and start creating and sharing now if you like, … but hold your sack-horses a second.  What about the other buttons, bells and whistles? Are they there just to look gizmo-ish? No no and thrice no.  The button on the right of the PlayStation®Vita system screen is your POPIT BUTTON, … we’ve met this chappy before, … but press it again as it really is a joy to see how the Popit menu resplendently unfolds when touched.  Observe how the BACK BUTTON appears over the Popit Menus. Stylish. I could press that all day long. Touch the back button to close the Popit menu.  As you know, … the tweak facility is meat and drink to a LittleBigPlanetian and the TWEAK BUTTON is found under the Popit menu button. Just a little prod of this allows you to faff around with any object already selected.  What else? The button at the ‘bottom' … right hand side of the screen opens up the flip menus.  The top button flips your object vertically, and the left button flips it horizontally.  Then there’s the COPY BUTTON, … dashed clever this one. There it is at the bottom left of your screen. Tap that and you can make facsimiles of your object as many times as you wish.  Now before you go and create objects devices, games and levels of unfathomable ingenuity, … wit and splendor,  I want to tell you about the CONTROLLINATOR BUTTON. Whenever you get into a Controllinator you’ll notice a button in the bottom left corner of the screen.  Very handy it is as, when pressed, it ejects you from the seat allowing you renewed freedom. Brilliant, as the kids never say.  There was something else too? Oh yes, Susan wants to say hello. Go on then. <SOUND FX : Cat meow.> NARRATOR (CHUCKLE) You flirt.

1168456128: The Shardinator is used to blast things into loads of pieces! If that sounds like fun, you should fetch one straight away from the Gadgets page in your Tools Bag. Just use the action button to place it onto the unlucky object. If you hook up some logic to the Shardinator and then trigger it, you’ll see its effect: boom! Lots of little shards. Of course, you can customize the destruction via the Shardinator’s tweak menu, so open it up with the menu button.  The Edge Cracks and Face Cracks tweaks control how many pieces the object will be broken into. Adjust them until you achieve the effect you want, but be careful not to overload your levels with too many bits!  If you want your pieces to go flying, it’s easy. Increase the Random Linear Velocity and Random Angular Velocity tweaks to send the shards into the stratosphere! Use the Trigger Delay tweak to make the Shardinator wait for the designated period of time before exploding once it’s triggered. The Lifespan tweak controls how long the shards will stay in the world after the explosion. By default, they’ll stay forever! Use the Shard Effect tweak to change the appearance of the initial explosion. If the shards are going to disappear, you can change the appearance of this as well using the Destroy Effect tweak. Activate the Dephysicalized Shards tweak to prevent the shards from bumping into anything. If you want the shards to be quiet, you can turn off their Physics Audio. And finally, if you want the shards to share a tag after the object explodes, activate the Assign Tag to Shards tag and set up your desired tag below!

The Plasma Projectile is instantly lethal, but it’s not affected by gravity.  The Water Projectile is a harmless water droplet. It is affected by gravity. 434399028: Nice rocket! Very retro.  Launch that beauty into the Imagisphere and Houston would, most definitely, NOT have a problem. However, during the meticulous pre-flight test, well Sackboy jumped on it to make sure it didn’t fall over, and a problem was found! Mission control down there on the PlayStation®Vita system say it needs a new Remote Tag Sensor. What in the blue blazes is one of those?, you cry.  Well, a Remote tag Sensor let’s you detect when a tag is activated in your level either on the PlayStation®3 system or the PlayStation®Vita system. Nifty hey? To demonstrate, earlier on, Sackboy set up the Tag on the PlayStation®Vita system. What you need to do is open Popit, select the Remote Tag Sensor, and pop it on the retro rocket. The next step is to take your Popit cursor and highlight the Remote Tag Sensor.  That’s the style. Now press the TWEAK button.  Note the colors. Make sure the color you select matches the color of the Tag on the PlayStation®Vita system. Color coordination is imperative for success here. Okay dokey, now wire the Remote Tag Sensor into the rocket’s Thruster. Good good. Then pick up your PlayStation®Vita system so mission control can pull that switch in 10, 9, 8, 7, 6, 5  --- No, I said five not fire ---but worry ye not, we have success. 2946379215: The Game Camera is used to ensure that the proper bits of your levels take centre stage. You can find them on the Tools page of your Tools Bag, so why not put one in the world and have a look?  Use the left stick and the menu button to open the Game Camera’s tweak menu. The first thing to do is to set up your shot, so select Angle & Zoom. Pan the shot around with the left stick. Tilt your shot with the right stick. If you make a mistake, you can push the sticks in to reset the shot and start over. Zoom the shot in and out with the left shoulder buttons, and roll the camera with the right shoulder buttons. Once you’ve set it up how you like, press the action button to make it so. Most cameras are triggered by player proximity. To customise the activation area for your camera, tweak the zone. Use the left stick to move the zone around and the right stick to resize it. The left shoulder buttons move the zone back and forth and the right shoulder buttons make the zone thicker and thinner. Once it’s right, press the action button. The Adjust Player Tracking tweak allows you to customise how much the camera will concentrate on a player’s movement. At 100%, it will keep track of your players pretty closely, but at 0% it will completely ignore them, and leave your shot exactly how you set it up. If you want your shot to change based on the game camera’s physical angle, tweak Local Space to yes. Otherwise your view will remain stable no matter what the camera’s doing. And for a bit of extra drama, you can make the camera shake a little… or a lot.  If you don’t want the camera to activate until all players are in its zone, use the Require All Players tweak. If you want your camera to be triggered by logic instead, you can change how it will behave with the Input Action tweak. In the Focus category, you can adjust your shot’s depth of field and whether this changes relative to players. Finally, you can turn Z Relative Camera on if you want the shot to adjust based on the camera’s position in the layers.

• Exclusive Costumes – dress up your sack-buddy as a Space Pirate Captain, Space Pilot, Space Prison Warden, Holo Sackboy or in a Space Walk Suit.
• New Items – customize your world with a batch of stickers, objects, materials and decorations.
• New Tools and Gadgets – make your own Cross-Controller games, or play levels made by other LBP fans.

3669382456: The Magic Mouth is the way to give your characters something to say! You can find it on the Creatures & Characters page of your Tools Bag, so grab one now and place it in the world with the action button.  A Magic Mouth isn’t going to do much without text, so enter its tweak menu with the menu button and add some speech using the Speech tweak. Next it’s time to decide how the Speech appears in the world once it’s triggered! Use the Display tweak to decide between a speech Bubble, a Subtitle, or Nothing at all, if you’d rather your line were heard and not seen. If you’re using a Bubble, you can change its appearance and position with the Bubble Style and Position on Screen tweaks. Use the Voice Type tweak to determine how the dialogue sounds. You can choose from an array of gibberish, or record your own speech! If your Magic Mouth is triggered by player proximity instead of logic, set up the size and shape of the Trigger Radius and Layer Detection Range tweaks. Use the Input Action tweak to determine how the Magic Mouth behaves once it’s triggered. In the behavior category you can change whether your speech closes automatically and whether a player can skip the speech altogether using the back button. The Movie Camera tweak lets you frame a nice camera shot for the duration of your dialogue. If your Magic Mouth needs to be associated with a Sackbot, you can assign that Sackbot’s actor name. You can also display the actor name on speech bubbles if you like! Finally, it’s worth knowing that every Magic Mouth has an output that produces a signal once it’s done delivering its line. You can use this to trigger anything, or string speeches together!

651605747: A Joystick Rotator is used in conjunction with a Controlinator to rotate an object based on the left or right stick. It’s found on the Gadgets page of your Tools Bag. Take one out, put it onto a Controlinator, and let’s find out how it works. The first thing to do is hook up the Controlinator to your Joystick Rotator. You can use either stick. There are separate inputs and outputs for left/right and up/down, so be sure to hook them up correctly!  Now hop into the Controlinator and wriggle the appropriate stick. The object will rotate to match your movements! Of course, you can customize this behavior somewhat, so pop back out of the Controlinator and open the Joystick Rotator’s tweak menu with the popit cursor and the menu button. First, if you want your object to rotate slower or faster, change its Rotation Speed. The Acceleration tweak controls how hard the Joystick Rotator tries to reach its top speed. Finally, the Input Action controls how the Joystick Rotator reacts to logic. You can simply turn it on and off, or you can adjust its strength or speed on the fly! Note that this tweak only applies to the bottom input of the Joystick Rotator – the inputs on the top and the side will always relate to rotation speed.

12817079: When you need something to simply pop from one layer to another, the In/Out Mover is the way to go. Find it on the Gadgets page of the Tools Bag. Place it on the object that needs moving using the left stick and the action button. Nothing happens! This is because an In/Out Mover needs an input before it does what it’s told. Let’s use a button – nice and simple. Now you’re ready to tweak the In/Out Mover. Just press the menu button. Change the Maximum Speed tweak to determine how quickly the object will move between layers. With Allow Pushing set to No, the object’s movement will stop if it bumps into anything. If you set Allow Pushing to Yes, the object will instead shove any obstructions through the layers – including players! For more control over what it can and can’t push, you can change the Maximum Weight that Can Be Pushed.  The Input Action tells the In/Out Mover which layer to move to when it receives an input. This can be set to move in or out a single layer, or it can be set to move to specific layers. Note that the object needs a steady input to make it to its destination – if the input gets cut off early, the object could wind up between layers!  Finally, if your logic needs to know where an In/Out Mover is, consider using its output, which will send signals based on its location. Try it out!

2214859563: If you don’t want to use a scoreboard to end a level in your adventure, you can use the Progress Board instead. Check it out on the Gameplay page of your Tools Bag. Once you’ve placed one in the world, you’ll need to make sure something is hooked up to its input – otherwise it won’t do anything! You can have anything you want end your level, from a simple button to a complicated series of quest completions.  Next you’ll want to open the Progress Board’s tweak menu using the popit cursor and the menu button. If you set up a Board Name, it appears on top of your Progress Board when it drops down. This can be a message of congratulations, a note about the story, or anything you like. If you don’t want to write a message, just leave it alone – it’ll still work. If the level you’re ending is the last level in your Adventure, change Ends Adventure to Yes. This will allow your players to rate your Adventure!  Next you can customise what your Progress Board displays – the score your players earned, how many collectabells they found, and things like that. Just highlight the right options using the action button and they’ll show up on the board. Like a classic scoreboard, Progress Boards can be stuffed full of gifts! You can give players three prize bubbles per category. The categories are as follows: First, the Aced Level Gifts. If a player beats your level without any deadly disasters, they’ll earn this lot. Second, the Collected All Gifts. These are for players who have found all the other prizes in your level. And lastly, the Level Complete Gifts. Everyone who finishes the level gets these. With the Where to Next tweak, you can determine whether the Progress Board sends your players to another level, or back to their pods. You can also set it to Return to Previous, which will place them back wherever they were when they entered the level. If you send them through a level link, you can set it up via the options below – just pick a level and, if applicable, an entrance label.

1641543354: The Global Water Tweaker is used to adjust your level’s water settings on the fly. It is found on the Gadgets page of your Tools Bag, so get one out and put it down!  Open the Global Water Tweaker’s tweak menu using the menu button. Raise or lower the water with the Water Level tweak. Give it waves – or not – with the Wave Height tweak. The Water Color tweak lets you change its color, and you can make it more or less cloudy with the Water Murkiness tweak. The Water Bits tweak adds sparkly debris to the water. Make the water transition loud or quiet using the Water Drain Sounds tweak. Turn the water light effects off with the Light Patterns tweak. If your Global Water Tweaker is being triggered by player proximity, you can increase or decrease the size of the trigger radius. Activate the Only Activate Once tweak if you want the water to change once, and then never again. Change the Transition Time to change how long it takes to change from the current water settings to the new ones once the Global Water Tweaker has been triggered. Finally, it’s worth noting that you can also trigger the Global Water Tweaker via logic. Just wire a button or whatever else into its input!

1639250291: Did you know you can use the touchpad on your controller to manipulate things in Create mode? It’s easy! Push in your touchpad to open up the Popit Menu, slide your finger up to highlight the Goodies Bag, and push in the touchpad again. Now browse the Goodies Bag with the power of touch until you highlight the object or material you want.  Push in the touchpad to make your choice. Now you can use one finger to move the object around your create space. You can also use two fingers – spread them apart to increase the object’s size, pinch them closer together to shrink it, or twist them to spin the object around. To place the object, push in the touchpad. To smear a material, keep the touchpad pushed in, press the L2 button, and move your finger around. To cut through a material, push in the touchpad and press the L1 button. It’s like magic!

1744240314: The Object Saver is used to preserve an object’s status between playthroughs. They’re on the Tools page of your Tools Bag. There are no fancy tweaks to fiddle with – an Object Saver is a one and done. If an object has an Object Saver on it, it will save its state when the player exits your level. When the player re-enters, the object will remember where it was and how it was positioned. It works on logic, too. Any triggered logic will remain triggered, and anything turned off will stay off.  It’s probably also worth mentioning that if an Object Saver is on an object that gets destroyed, it will remember that, too. When the player re-enters the level, the object will still be gone!

1492632121: An Advanced Rotator makes things spin in any direction its logic tells it to. Grab one from the Gadgets page in your Tools Bag and place it onto something. Unlike a normal Rotator, the Advanced Rotator doesn’t kick in right away. It requires an input from logic to do anything. Let’s hook this one up to a 3-way switch. Play with the switch and observe as the object spins around in either direction! The stronger the signal it receives, the faster it goes. Of course, there are tweaks to play with as well, so open up the Advanced Rotator’s tweak menu using the menu button. First, if you want your object to rotate slower or faster, change its Rotation Speed. Next, the strength category! Tweak the Advanced Rotator’s acceleration and deceleration to change how hard it tries to reach its top speed and how easily it can slow itself down. Finally, the Input Action allows you to change how the Advanced Rotator reacts to logic. You can use it to turn the Advanced Rotator on and off, or adjust its strength and speed on the fly. Note that this only applies to the bottom input. The input on the side always applies to rotation speed!

2641756569: A Broadcast Microchip will project all of its logic onto other things. They’re on the Gadgets page of your Tools Bag, so put one down and let’s have a look. First, place any logic you like onto the Broadcast Microchip's circuit board. The Broadcast Microchip will automatically start broadcasting that logic to its target. By default, it will target the nearest player, so just move closer to see it work its magic. Naturally, you can change its target via the tweak menu, so open that up with the menu button. With the Broadcast Targets tweak, you can tell the Broadcast Microchip to target creatures, tags, or everything. If you select creatures, you can specify a certain character with the Character to Detect option below. Similarly, when you select tags, you can specify which tag. With the Broadcast To tweak, determine whether the Broadcast Microchip chooses the closest target in range, every target in range, or just things in contact with whatever the Broadcast Microchip is placed on. If your Broadcast Microchip has a range, you can tweak it in the range category below. It’s worth knowing that setting a Maximum Detection Range to below zero will make its range infinite! The trigger category will appear if your Broadcast Microchip targets things in contact. Use these tweaks to change the way the Broadcast Microchip handles detection via contact. Finally, like a normal Microchip, a Broadcast Microchip can be turned on and off via its input. You can put any logic you like onto a Broadcast Microchip, from simple tags, crazy movement, or complex customized control schemes. Start small, and soon you’ll be ready to broadcast with the best of them. Have fun!

753971530: When you need two things to stick together, the simplest answer is Gluing. Gluing is so simple that you can do it using only the popit cursor!  When you want to glue two things together, select one of them with the popit cursor using the left stick and the action button. Position the first object so that it’s touching the second one. Be sure they’re touching! Then just hold down the action button… and boom! After a moment the two objects become one. If you want to separate them again, just select one of them and press the delete button. Don’t worry, if you only press it once you won’t actually delete anything! Gluing objects across layers is slightly trickier, but still pretty simple. Select one thing like before and position it so that both objects are touching across layers. Next, hold down the relevant shuffle button to nudge your selected object into the other. If you’re doing it correctly, you will see the object you’re nudging against change color. Now just hold down the action button as well… and boom again! They’re together at last. Finally, for a more precise method of Gluing, you can use the Advanced Glue Tool instead. It’s on the Tools page of your Tools Bag. With the Advanced Glue Tool selected, you can glue two touching objects together simply by hovering your cursor over one of them, pressing the action button, and repeating the process with the second one. Glue one, glue the other, and you’re done! They’re glued together. The method you use most is up to you. Either way, you’re ready to glue like a pro!

1111155684: The Sackpocket Item Sensor gives a signal when it detects a player who possesses one of your adventure’s sackpocket items. It’s on the Creatures & Characters page of your Tools Bag, so grab one now and have a look. The first thing you’ll need to do is pick which item the Sackpocket Item Sensor is looking for. Tweak the sensor using the menu button, highlight the Choose Adventure Item tweak, and press the action button. Here you’ll see all the usual powerups, plus any other items you’ve created yourself.  Highlight your favorite and press the action button. Use the Required Quantity tweak to change how many copies of the item your players need to have for the Sackpocket Item Sensor to give a signal. For most powerups, you’ll just leave this number at 1. If the Only When Item is Activated tweak is set to Yes, the Sackpocket Item Sensor will only detect the item when the player currently has it equipped! In the Range category you can set up how large an area the sensor is searching. It’s worth noting that if you set the Maximum Detection Range tweak to below zero, it will detect an infinite range instead. Useful for global logic! Finally, use the Invert Output tweak to detect when a player doesn’t possess an item instead.
2041043065: The Projectile Sensor produces a signal after the object it’s on has been bombarded by projectiles like plasma balls and water drops! It can be found on the Gameplay page of your Tools Bag. Grab one now and place it in the path of a projectile! Notice how the Projectile Sensor’s output lights up once it gets hit? That’s the Projectile Sensor in its most basic form. You can wire up that output to any logic you want! Now let’s check out its tweaks in the tweak menu. Open it up with the menu button. Increase the Target Count tweak to change how many shots the Projectile Sensor can take before it produces a full signal. If you don’t want it to start counting from zero, change the Current Count tweak! If you want the count to reset back to zero once it’s full, activate the Reset When Full tweak. The Projectile Types Detected tweak determines whether the Projectile Sensor reacts to all projectiles, or only a specific one. If the object your sensor is on is part of a larger whole, activating the Include Rigid Connections tweak will allow the Projectile Sensor to detect projectiles hitting any of its parts. Finally, invert the Projectile Sensor’s output if you want it to turn off after it gets hit by a projectile instead!

Here you have it: a blank canvas for your adventure, ready to be filled with levels and decorated to your heart’s content. From here, you can place blank levels with the action button or, if you’ve already made levels and saved them, import levels using the menu button. Once levels are placed, you can edit, customise or delete them directly from your Adventure Map. No need to go back to your Moon! Now let’s get to decorating. Press the right stick to open up the Adventure Map menu. The Terrain Material page and Border Material page are used to change the materials your map is made of. Note that if you choose a colour tweakable material, you can tweak it from the menu!  The Stickers and Decorations pages allow you to plaster your Adventure Map with colourful, crazy nonsense. It works just like normal Create – just move them with the left stick and press the action button to put them down.  At the top of the menus, you can save an Adventure Map for later or reset your current map back to the defaults. Any maps you do save can be loaded from the My Maps page! With the Landscape Styles page, you can choose from a variety of layouts for your Adventure Map’s landscape. Just select your favourite with the action button. The Global Controls page is similar to the one in your levels – from here you can adjust your map’s lighting and ambient audio. Finally, press the pause button and select the Details option in order to give your Adventure Map a name, a description, and a lovely sticker.

The Can Be Blocked setting toggles whether the wind stops when it hits an object or if it ignores obstructions and blows right through. The Effect Type tweak lets you change whether objects in the wind behave as if they’re being sucked or blown. Finally, you can attach logic to the wind via its input, and change the Input Action to use logic to turn it on and off, affect the wind’s strength, or its speed. 351515623: When you’ve made something amazing and you want to share it with the world, a Prize Bubble is just the thing. Find one on the Gameplay page of your Tools Bag and place it in the world with the action button. Before it’s filled, a Prize Bubble is basically just a big Score Bubble. It’s even worth fifty points! To give it a prize, enter its tweak menu using the popit cursor and the menu button. Make it static if you don’t want it to roll away, and then move down to the Prize tweak. Press the action button to open up your My Objects and My Stickers pages. From here, scroll around until you find the item you want to give away, then just press the action button again! Your Prize Bubble is now filled. You can even see it floating inside, waiting to be collected. Activate the Shareable tweak if you want other players to be able to spread your prize around to their friends. Finally, it’s worth knowing that when a Prize Bubble is triggered by logic, it’ll behave just as if the activating player had bumped into it personally!
656244747: The Score Bubble is the classic way of letting your players earn points in a level! You can find them on the Gameplay page of your Tools Bag. Place one in the world with the action button! The Score Bubble will be collected by whichever player touches it first. If a player collects lots of Score Bubbles in a row, they’ll earn combo multipliers for even more points! Now open up the Score Bubble’s tweak menu using the popit cursor and the menu button. Make it static if you don’t want it to roll away, and then change the Score Value tweak if you want a Score Bubble to be worth a certain amount of points! By default, they’re worth ten. Finally, it’s worth knowing that when a Score Bubble is triggered by logic, the activating player collects its points as if they had bumped into it personally.

2394957288: An Advanced Mover moves the object it’s attached to based on the logic signals it receives. Find one on the Gadgets page of your Tools Bag and pop it onto an object now.  Without a signal, the Advanced Mover doesn’t do much. Let’s use a 3-way switch to demonstrate how it works. First, attach the switch to the Left/Right input on the side of the Advanced Mover. Observe how the object moves left and right as you pull the switch back and forth. Similarly, if you attach the switch to the Up/Down input on the top, playing with the switch makes the object move up and down. Now use the popit cursor and the menu button to open the Advanced Mover’s tweak menu. Change the Speed tweak to determine the Advanced Mover’s top speed. The Local Space tweak changes whether an Advanced Mover determines its directions based on the rest of the world – up is always up, left is always left – or whether it determines directions based on the orientation of the Advanced Mover.  Next, the strength category! Tweak the Advanced Mover’s acceleration and deceleration to change how hard it tries to reach its top speed. Finally, the Input Action determines how the Advanced Mover reacts to logic. You can simply turn it on and off, or adjust its speed or strength on the fly! Note that this only applies to the bottom input – the Left/Right input and the Up/Down input always do the same thing.

516731861: The State Sensor outputs a signal when it detects certain characters performing actions. For example, it could output a signal whenever OddSock jumps or whenever Small Toggle grabs something. You can find it on the Creatures & Characters page of your Tools Bag. Place one down now and take a look. Open the State Sensor’s tweak menu with the menu button. The first thing you’ll see is the Choose State tweak. Open it up with the action button and check out all the options! Each of these represents an action the State Sensor can be used to detect. Select Running and then run around a bit. Notice that it lights up whenever your Sackperson runs by. Use the Detect State Of tweak to change whether it’s detecting the state of characters in range or whether it only looks for characters in contact with whatever the sensor is placed on. In the menus below, depending on what you pick, you will either be able to customize the detection radius or how it treats things in contact. If you only want a certain character’s states to be observed, use the Character to Detect tweak to open up your level’s Characters page and select the right one. If you change your mind, just use the Reset button! If you’d rather it gave a signal when a character isn’t doing something, rather than when they are doing it, just use Invert Output. Finally, if you place the State Sensor directly onto a character or onto a Broadcast Microchip, it will gain a new option: Sense Owner Only. With this activated, the State Sensor will only ever detect what the character it’s been placed on is up to. Handy stuff!

3433718141: The Rail Hook latches onto Bendy Rails and moves along them. That means if you attach something to a Rail Hook, you can make anything follow a Bendy Rail! Take a look; they’re on the Gameplay page of the Tools Bag. Place a Rail Hook into the world like anything else. Note that if you move it near a Bendy Rail, it will latch onto it automatically! Now it will travel back and forth from one end of the Bendy Rail to the other. Naturally, you can tweak this movement however you like. Just hover the cursor over the Rail Hook and press the menu button. If you want the movement of a Rail Hook to be purely physics-based, set it to be non-motorized. It will no longer move automatically and will instead be pulled along the rail by gravity and other physical forces. Otherwise, leave it set to motorized. Make the Rail Hook move slower or faster using the Speed tweak. If you want it to linger at each end for a while, use the Pause tweak. Setting the Reversed tweak to Yes will swap which ends the Rail Hook begins and finishes on. In the Strength settings, you can change how quickly the Rail Hook accelerates and decelerates.  Now let’s take a look at the Rail Hook’s inputs. The first input is the Engage/Disengage input, and with this input you can use logic to make your Rail Hooks attach to and detach from Bendy Rails. Give it a try – you can even set them up to hop from rail to rail! The other input is the usual sort, and can be tweaked from the Rail Hook’s tweak menu. With this input, you can use logic to turn Rail Hooks on and off, make them move faster or slower, and other helpful tweaks.  Finally, you can make Rail Hooks invisible and silent with the Visible in Play Mode and Mute tweaks.

3476453230: Let’s take a look at the Organizertron and how to add quests to your own adventures. You can do it from the Organizertron page of the Global Stuff, or you can do it from the Organizertron itself in Create! Open it up now. The first thing you need to do is Add a Quest. Once you do, it appears in the Organizertron, ready to be tweaked. Highlight the quest and press the menu button to get started. First, decide whether your quest is a Primary Quest. If it is, the Organizertron will highlight it as such so that your players know it’s extra important.  Next, you can make your quests invisible! An invisible quest can be used for behind-the-scenes logic, or you can reveal them later on for surprise objectives.  If you’re going to have a bunch of quests, it might be worth giving them different categories! You can use the Current Category tweak to create a new category or choose from a list of the ones you’ve already set up. When one quest is dependent on another, a player won’t be able to see it until they’ve completed the quest it’s dependent on. You can use the Test Quest menu to activate, complete, and deactivate your quests on the fly to make sure all of your logic is working correctly. You can test your quest tracking from here as well. It’s a good idea to give your quests names, so highlight the Quest Title, press the action button, and think of something catchy. For further detail, you can change the quest description as well – something to remind players what they’re in for! Below that, you can give the quest objectives, if you like. Once a quest’s objectives are completed, the quest is completed, too – so objectives are a good way of guiding your players through a quest. Simple quests don’t need any objectives at all, but for the really busy ones you can add up to sixteen of them! You can give each objective its own name to remind players how to complete it. The Number of completions required tweak lets you decide how many times an objective must be done before it counts as complete. Want your players to catch seventeen chickens? Need them to push a button forty-two times? You’re covered. Like quests themselves, objectives can be made invisible for behind-the-scenes bookkeeping or to be revealed later. Also like quests, you can test individual objectives to make sure they’re working correctly! If you want to be rid of an objective, you can easily delete it from here as well. Finally, scroll to the right to set up the prizes your players earn once they complete your quest. It’s okay if you leave these empty though – the quest will function either way!

2856522198: The Material Tweaker is used to alter the properties of the materials in your levels. It’s on the Gadgets page of your Tools Bag, so get one out and put it on some material. With no tweaks selected, the Material Tweaker doesn’t do anything, so open up its tweak menu with the menu button. Use the Grabbability tweak to determine if the material is grabbable by one player, many players, or nobody at all. The Grabbable By tweak is helpful if your level uses the motion controller – it determines whether the material can be grabbed by Sackthings, the Move cursor, or both.  If you want the material to be climbable, activate the climbable tweak. To make the material bouncy, increase the Bouncy tweak. Decrease the Friction tweak to make the material slippery. Change the Stickiness tweak to determine whether things stick to the material, and activate the Indestructible tweak to ensure that nothing can break the material. Activate the Remove Bevel tweak to turn off a material’s bevel. Toggle a material’s shadow with the Cast Shadows tweak. These options are purely visual, so just use what looks good! To make the material silent as it bumps around, turn off the Physics Sounds tweak. Finally, you can use logic to turn the Material Tweaker on and off via its input.

1627970875: The Player Sensor produces a signal when a player enters its detection radius. You can find them on the Creatures & Characters page of your Tools Bag, so fetch one now and place it in the world using the action button. See how it lights up whenever you wander near it? That’s the Player Sensor at its simplest. Use it to open doors, play sounds, or whatever else you like! Of course, you can customise the behaviour. Just hover over the Player Sensor with the popit cursor and press the menu button to open its tweak menu. First, you can change the sensor’s minimum and maximum detection radius. You can also change the angle of the radius and how many layers thick it is. Use these tweaks to ensure you know exactly where your players need to be for the sensor to detect them. Next, if you only want the Player Sensor to activate when it detects more than one player, you can adjust the Number of Players Required tweak. You can also just activate the Require All Players tweak if you want it to look for everyone! If it is looking for everyone, the Detects unspawned players tweak determines whether it looks for characters who are currently waiting to respawn from a Checkpoint. Use the Character to Detect option to open the characters menu and select a specific character for the player sensor to detect. If you change your mind, just use the reset button. Finally, you can invert the sensor's output so that it only turns off when it sees a player instead.

72464762: Velociporters are a fun and fast way of teleporting a Sackthing from one spot to another. Find them on the Gameplay page of your Tools Bag and place one in the world. Actually, place two of them – they aren’t much good unless they’re in pairs! Jump into one, pop out the other. They’ll also keep your momentum. That’s the magic of Velociporters! Let’s take a peek at the tweak menu. Hover the popit cursor over one of the Velociporters and press the menu button. Velociporters will always teleport a player to the nearest Velociporter of the same color and label. You can change those colors and labels from here. Note that labels are only necessary if you have a lot of Velociporters – you don’t have to use them. By default, a Velociporter shines with the color it’s associated with. You can turn this off with the Show Velociporter Color tweak. You can also turn off the teleport noise with the Audio tweak! Finally, it’s worth knowing that you can use logic to turn individual Velociporters on and off!

845319183: The Collectabell is a brand-new form of currency for LittleBigPlanet. In an adventure, unlike points from score bubbles, players keep their Collectabell totals from level to level. Collectabells are also persistent, so once you’ve collected them from a level they’ll be gone forever! You can find the Collectabells on the Gameplay page of your Tools Bag. Grab one now and pop it into the world with the action button! Like a score bubble, to collect a Collectabell, a player simply needs to run into it. Hide them throughout your adventure wherever you like.  Now open up the Collectabell’s tweak menu using the popit cursor and the menu button. Make it static if you don’t want it rolling around and then move to the Score Value tweak. Use this tweak to determine how many Collectabells an individual Collectabell is worth. You can change their colors, too! Finally, one last tip: if a Collectabell receives an input via logic, it will be collected as if a player ran into it!

3883148572: A wave generator produces a signal in a wave back and forth between its minimum signal value to its maximum signal value. It’s pretty simple to understand once you see it in action, so grab one from the Gadgets page in your Tools Bag and slap it down. If you don’t already know, now’s a good time to learn about signal waveforms and how to observe them. Move your popit cursor over the wave generator’s output using the left stick, then press the R2 button. Now you can see the wave generator’s signal output in action – from -100 to 100 and back again, over and over, nice and smooth. This output can be connected to anything from movers to timers to lights! Of course, you can tweak the wave generator like anything else. Open the tweak menu using the menu button. With the Period tweak, you can lengthen or shorten the time it takes for the signal to go from one end to the other. The Sync tweak changes the timing of the wave generator relative to the timing in the rest of your level. You can use the Delay tweak to make the signal pause for a while at each end. Change the wave generator’s Input Action to determine how it reacts to other inputs. This could be as simple as turning the wave generator on and off or as complicated as feeding the wave generator specific position values. In the Output category, you can change the wave generator’s maximum and minimum signal values – the signal can start and end wherever you like! You can also invert the output. Just keep an eye on the signal waveform and you’ll have it set up just right in no time.

233426802: The Interactive Live Stream Sensor is a fancy new tool for letting your player's live stream audience join in the fun. You can find it on the Gadgets page of your Tools Bag, so fetch one now and place it in the world. Open up the Interactive Live Stream Sensor's tweak menu and take a look. The first tweak you'll see is the Chat Sample Time tweak. This is how long the viewers will have to type their choices into the live stream chat once they've been prompted to do so.  In the chat labels category, you can set up to five Key Phrases for the viewers to choose from. Make them short and snappy if you want them to type them in time! They'll be prompted after the Interactive Live Stream Sensor receives an signal from its left input. After the sample time is over, the sensor will examine the results of the chat and produce an output based on the results, which you can wire up to anything in your level that you like. The winning result will produce a full signal, and the runners up will produce analogue values based their popularity.  Use the behavior category to determine whether the sensor produces its output only after the full duration of the sample time, or continuously!  Finally, if you want to tally the votes fresh each time, you can reset them by attaching some logic to the Interactive Live Stream Sensor's reset input.

2545504479: Tag Radar may sound like the name of an alien private detective, but it is in fact a facility to track movement on either the PlayStation®3 system or PlayStation®Vita system and use that information to make something move on the other screen.   Yes yes, that sounds as clear as mud, I know, but this tricky maze will allow me to demonstrate.   So, take a gander at the PlayStation®Vita system screen.   You will see the maze that is also on the PlayStation®3 system screen. But what’s the difference?   Exactly!   On the PlayStation®Vita system there’s a tag on the box and a new chip which is the Tag Radar! Well spotted.   Give it a little tweak why don’t you?   Bring up your Popit cursor, highlight the Tag Radar chip and press the TWEAK button. You must ensure the tag type matches the color of the tag on the box.   Well done.   Now, let’s move to the PlayStation®3 system and make the magic happen there too. Open up your Popit menu and select the Tag Radar from your Tools Bag. Place it on the maze in a similar spot to where it is on the PlayStation®Vita system screen.   Bring out your Popit cursor and tweak the Tag Radar and set it to ‘Receive’. Observe the ghost of the Tag that’s from the PlayStation®Vita system.  It’s not really a ghost, I just said that word to inject some mild peril.  Touch the box on the PlayStation®Vita system.  You see!  When you move it on the PlayStation®Vita system the Ghost Tag moves on the PlayStation®3 system. You liking that?  Try placing the box on the button. It’s great isn’t it. I can literally hear your brain whizzing with possibilities.  You go for it, squire.

1715904997: Materials are the foundation of any level, so you’ll need to know how to place them in the world.  The materials are kept in your goodies bag! Open it up. There are various kinds of materials to choose from, separated into categories such as Cardboard, Sponge, and Glass. Each type of material has different properties, but for now just choose one that looks nice. Now pick the shape you’ll use to stamp the material into the world. Before you place the material, you can adjust its position with the left stick, change its orientation with the right stick, move it in and out of the layers using the shuffle button, and make them thicker and thinner with the thickness buttons. Once it looks right, place it into the world with the action button. And there it is! If you want to change it, simply point at it with the popit cursor and pick it up again with the action button. To make a copy of your material, push in the left stick. To flip it around, push in the right stick. To delete it, just press the delete button. But that’s not all! With a shape selected, you can also smear the material by holding down the action button and moving the left stick. Or you can cut a swath through the old stuff by holding down the delete button instead. Finally, every material has a tweak menu, which you can access by pressing the menu button. The Position in Layer tweak changes a material’s position in its current layer. You can move it back and forth. Note that this is a purely visual distinction, intended mostly for art purposes.  You can also change a material’s physics properties from dynamic to static, which means they won’t move no matter what.  Some materials also allow you to change their colors! This is indicated by the color wheel on their icon in the popit.  Finally, if you have the perfect shape made out of the wrong stuff, you can easily change materials. Just find the material you want and select the Material Changer tool. Then just use the popit cursor and the action button! Now you’re ready to build levels like a pro.

1421644559: The Global Audio Tweaker is used to change your level’s audio settings on the fly. You can find it on the Gadgets page of your Tools Bag, so snatch one up and place it in the world.  Open up the Global Audio Tweaker’s tweak menu using the menu button. From here you can change the qualities of your level’s sounds and music.  In the Audio category, the Choose Ambience tweak lets you choose from a set of background ambient settings. You can make your level sound like it’s in a jungle, a spaceship, or all sorts of other things! The SFX Volume tweak makes your level’s sound effects louder or quieter. You can also adjust the volume of your background ambience, your level’s music, and your level’s dialogue! The Reverb Settings category lets you change the resonance of your level’s sounds. The Reverb Setting tweak allows you to select the quality of resonance to apply to your sounds, and the other tweaks allow you to apply this effect to the sound effects, music, or dialogue in your level. The Low-Pass Filter Settings category lets you apply a low-pass filter to the sound effects, music, or dialogue in your level. In simple terms, this makes a noise sound muffled, like you’re hearing it underwater. The High-Pass Filter Settings category does the same, but with a high-pass filter. This makes a noise sound hissy, like music from a faraway radio. By default, a Global Audio Tweaker is activated by player proximity. You can also trigger it via logic, but if you’re using proximity you can increase or decrease the trigger radius. Activate the Only Activate Once tweak if you only want to trigger the new noise settings once. Finally, the Transition Time tweak determines how long it takes for the new settings to take effect once the Global Audio Tweaker has been triggered.

2633585671: When you need fancy transitions and dramatic angles, the movie cameras are the tool for you. Check them out in the Tools Bag.  The first thing you’ll want to do is change the angle and zoom of your shot. Tweak the movie camera and open up the Angle & Zoom function with the action button. Now you can adjust the shot to your liking.  Pan the shot around with the left stick. Tilt your shot with the right stick. If you make a mistake, you can push the sticks in to reset the shot and start over. Zoom the shot in and out with the left shoulder buttons, and roll the camera with the right shoulder buttons. Once you’ve set it up how you like, press the action button to seal the deal.  Want even more customisation? Down in the Focus category, you can adjust your shot’s depth of field and its flatness.  By default, a movie camera triggers when players enter its zone. You can trigger them with logic, too, but if you’re using the zone you can tweak its size and shape with the shoulder buttons and the left and right sticks.  The Transition Type determines what it looks like to switch from one shot to the next. By default it’s a simple, instantaneous cut, but play around with this tweak and you can wind up with all manner of fanciness.  You can change how long the cameras take to transition down in the Timing category.  Change a movie camera’s hold time to determine how long your shot lingers, or disable the hold time altogether to keep your shot indefinitely. If you do use a hold time, the movie camera’s output will produce a signal! Use this to string multiple movie cameras together.  If you want a movie camera to keep an eye on your players instead of a shot you set up yourself, tweak Track Player to Yes. Otherwise, leave it on No. If you want your shot to change based on the movie camera’s physical angle, tweak Local Space to yes. Otherwise your view will remain stable no matter what the camera’s doing. Similarly, you can turn Z Relative Camera on if you want the shot to adjust based on the camera’s position in the layers. And for a bit of extra drama, you can make the camera shake a little… or a lot!  Finally, it’s worth having a look at how movie cameras behave on sequencers. You can overlap them to create transitions; the transitions will last as long as they’re overlapped. This is a fantastic way of setting up long, complex cutscenes. Try it out!

Grab one from the Gameplay page in your Tools Bag and set it down with the action button to try it out. Open up the Layer Launcher’s tweak menu using the menu button. The Air Steering tweak determines how much control a Sackthing has over their movement when they’re being launched. At 100% they can move around as they like. Use the Trigger Automatically tweak to determine whether Sackthings launch immediately upon touching a Layer Launcher or whether they have to activate it by pressing the action button! 2104078776: An Impact Sensor on an object gives a signal when something bumps into its object. It’s on the Gadgets page of your Tools Bag, so grab one and have a look. Just place it into the world with the left stick and the action button. Notice how it turns on and off as your Sackthing jumps around on it, and how dropping a box onto it makes it turn on and stay on. That is the Impact Sensor’s basic behavior, but of course we can tweak it. Use the popit cursor and the menu button to open its tweak menu. If you only want an Impact Sensor to trigger via impacts with a certain character, use the Character to Detect option and choose from the Characters menu. If you change your mind, use the Reset button to clear your choice out. If your object consists of a lot of different pieces, all glued together, set Include Rigid Connections to Yes. This will ensure that the Impact Sensor detects impacts on all of its parts, rather than just the part you place it on. Change the Trigger Angle Range to tell the Impact Sensor to only detect impacts in a certain range. Using this you can easily only detect impacts from the top or the sides if you like… Otherwise just leave it at 360! Use the Include Touching tweak to enable the detection of impacts in adjacent thin layers. It is also used to detect when something is touching an object that has no collision, like Sticker Panel or Hologram.  If you set up a Tag in the Require Tag tweak, the Impact Sensor will only detect objects with that Tag. In the Collisions tweak you can set the Impact Sensor to detect only players, only the lead player, or anything.  Finally, you can invert the Impact Sensor’s output to make it only produce a signal when it’s not impacting anything!

769063984: Playlists are a brand-new way to group levels together. With a Playlist you’ll always have quick access to your favourite levels, and you can browse everyone else’s Playlists for undiscovered gems. To create a new Playlist, go to the My Playlists screen from your Profile screen. There, press the Create Playlist button. From here, you can search for the levels you want to add to your Playlist. Once you’ve found one, just highlight it and add it to your Playlist with the menu button! Each Playlist can hold up to 40 levels. If you change your mind about one of your choices, just select it and press the delete button to get rid of it.  If you want to reorder a level in your Playlist, select the Move option and use the left stick to reposition the level, and then use the action button to place it. To find new Playlists to browse, you can use the Community search function, view highly rated Playlists, or view a user’s Playlists directly from their Profile page! As you examine a Playlist, you can queue all its levels so you can play them later, play an individual right away, access a level creator’s Planet, and heart the list itself. With Playlists you’re able to easily explore quality levels with similar gameplay or themes. Have fun!

Grab one from the Gadgets page of your Tools Bag and use the left stick and the action button to place it in the world. Hook up the battery to something using its output. It’s as simple as that! Now it’s active and nothing can stop it! Open the Battery’s tweak menu using the menu button. If you’re working with more complicated logic that uses percentage values, you can customize the Battery’s output using the Output tweak. You can set it anywhere from 100% to negative 100%. 573175508: In the real world slapping stickers on anything and everything is frowned upon, and rightly so. Have you ever tried peeling a sticker off a cat? Susan was not amused. However, in the world of LittleBigPlanet™ we like to do things differently, yes, that means you’re free to sticker whatever you want. Even your bestest of chums or most fearsome of foes. Simply bring up ye POPIT with the MENU BUTTON and select STICKERS AND DECORATIONS using the LEFT STICK and the ACTION BUTTON. When you pick a sticker you’ll see it’s now at the end of your POPIT CURSOR, move it around with the LEFT STICK. You can resize and even give it a bit of a spin using the RIGHT STICK. Once you’re happy a quick press of the ACTION BUTTON stamps your sticker down. Or, if you're feeling adventurous, you can  use the nifty TOUCH PAD feature to move your sticker, placing it with a quick click!  Marvellous. As always, close the POPIT with a press of the BACK BUTTON and away you go.

Once you select the Capture Object tool with the action button, your cursor will become a box. Position the box over your object with the left stick. 3550087466: The Music Sequencer is a powerful tool that allows you to compose your own catchy tunes! You can find this powerful tool on the Music page of your Tools Bag, so grab one and put it in the world. Like a normal Gameplay Sequencer, the Music Sequencer consists of a customizable panel of alternating stripes of dark and light colors. Each of these stripes represents a length of time as the Music Sequencer plays from left to right. Unlike a normal Gameplay Sequencer, a Music Sequencer is used in conjunction with Sequencer Instruments to make lovely melodies. Place a Sequencer Instrument onto the panel now. Once an instrument is on the Music Sequencer, open up the Pattern Editor pressing the menu button.  Move the cursor around with the left stick and place notes with the action button. Pressing up or down on the right stick will change the note’s volume, and pressing left or right will change its timbre. R1 and L1 are used to lengthen and shorten the note. Use the left and right buttons to undo and redo as usual, and the up button to play or pause a preview of your composition. The down button lets you switch between eight notes per beat and six notes per beat. Press the menu button again to tweak an instrument’s pattern. From here you can change the qualities of the sound, from its volume and reverb to the key and scale it uses. Once you have one instrument set up, you’re well on your way to composing a whole song by filling the Music Sequencer with complementary and overlapping Sequencer Instruments. They’ll play all at once as the Music Sequencer progresses, so it’s up to you to make something that sounds wonderful! The Music Sequencer itself also has a number of tweaks to consider. You can give the panel multiple volume sliders if you want to keep some of your instruments hushed. Of course you can change its Trigger Radius if it’s activated by player proximity. Change its Tempo to make it play slower or faster, and use the Swing tweak to give a bounce to your beat. If you want the song to repeat once it’s reached the end, make it a Loop. Finally, the effects category. These settings control the amount of echo throughout your whole track, as well as the reverb type!

3666936100: A Selector has multiple outputs, only one of which can be active at a time. Find one on the Gadgets page of your Tools Bag and place it in the world with the action button. By default, a Selector’s first output is active. However, if you attach a button to its third input and push it, the first output will turn off and the third one with activate instead. If you then attach the button to the second input and push it, the same thing happens, and you’re left with just the second input active.  If you attach the button to the cycle input at the bottom and push it a few times, you’ll notice that it cycles from one input to the next, round and round!  Now open up the Selector’s tweak menu with the menu button. From here, you can increase or decrease the number of outputs the Selector has, as well as change which output is active to start. Finally, you can invert the Selector’s output – now only one output will be inactive at a time instead!

2585543740: The Look At Rotator rotates the object it’s placed on to make it face towards Sackthings or tags. Grab one from the Gadgets page of your Tools Bag and place it onto an object with the action button. By default, Look At Rotators react to players, so right away you can see the object start pointing itself towards you. Naturally, this behavior can be tweaked – just use the cursor and the menu button to open the tweak menu. The Rotation Speed tweak determines how fast the Look At Rotator rotates. The Acceleration tweak determines how hard it tries to reach its top speed. The Look At Rotator only points itself at things in its detection radius. In the Trigger category, you can change its minimum and maximum detection range, the angle of its detection range, and how many layers it can see. The Input Action tweak changes how the Look At Rotator reacts to logic. You can simply turn it on and off, or you can adjust its speed or strength on the fly. Finally, you can set up the Look At Rotator to pay attention to characters or tags. If you want it to look at a specific character, just use the Character to Detect option and select the appropriate character from the Characters page. Similarly, if it follows a tag, you can specify the tag right from the tweak menu!

4124519211: The Character Changer is a simple way to allow your players to change from one character to another. Grab one from the Gameplay page of your Tools Bag and place it in the world with the action button. A Character Changer won’t do much without a character to change into, so open up its tweak menu with the menu button and select the Character to Spawn As tweak. From here, select a character from your Characters page by highlighting it and pressing the action button. Now you can change into that character by standing in front of the Character Changer and activating it! If you want more than one character in your Character Changer, activate the Multiple Characters tweak and add a second character same as the first. Now you can change between them by activating the Character Changer repeatedly! If you change your mind about which characters you’ve chosen, you can remove both of them with the Reset button. Finally, it’s worth mentioning that you can also activate a Character Changer via logic rather than via player interaction! Just wire something into its input.

3318489578: The Anti-Gravity Tweaker changes the gravity of the object it’s placed on. Find one on the Gadgets page of your Tools Bag and put it on something with the action button. Observe how the object now floats about like a drifting spaceship! Bump it around a bit and watch it go. That’s the Anti-Gravity Tweaker in its simplest form, but let’s take a peek at some tweaks! Open up its tweak menu with the popit cursor and the menu button.  The Anti-Gravity tweak controls the strength of the anti-gravity effect. Turn it down a bit and the object will fall down, but it’ll still be nice and floaty.  Increase the Damping tweak to give the object resistance against motion. The higher the Damping, the more effort required to move it. Turn it all the way up to 100% and the object won’t move at all. Note that movement between layers is unaffected by Damping.  The Zero Buoyancy tweak controls how buoyant the object is in water. Outside of water, it will have no effect! Finally, the Input Action tweak controls how the Anti-Gravity Tweaker reacts to logic. You can simply turn it on and off, or you can adjust the anti-gravity strength on the fly!

3029356583: To create something wonderful, you’ll need to know how to place objects in the world and what to do with them once they’re there. Let’s have a go at it, shall we? Objects are kept in your goodies bag on the Collected Objects page.  Objects are separated into categories so you’ll always be able to find what you’re looking for. For now, anything will do, so just pick something enticing with the action button. Using the left stick, you can position your object before you place it, while the right stick is used to spin and resize it. The shuffle buttons move the object back and forth in the layers. You can put it anywhere! Once you’ve got it how you want it, place it into the world with the action button. Congratulations! You made something. If you want to fiddle with it again, you can pick it up with the popit cursor and the action button. To make a copy of the object, push in the left stick. To flip the object around, push in the right stick. Which brings us to the tweak menu. Everything has its own tweak menu, and you can open them up by pressing the menu button. Basic objects like this one only have a couple of tweak options, but some allow you to choose colors and brightness! These are indicated by the color wheels on their popit icons. The Position in Layer tweak changes an object’s position in its current layer. You can move it back and forth. Note that this is a purely visual distinction, intended mostly for art purposes.  The Physics Properties tweak determines whether an object is dynamic or static. A static object won’t move anywhere, no matter what.  Now you can fill your levels with all manner of wild and wacky stuff!

3031650777: In LittleBigPlanet, a MOTION RECORDER can record - wait for it - the motion of any object in your scene. You can do simple movement or even mind-melting animation. Let's melt some minds! Fetch a MOTION RECORDER from the MOVERS section of your TOOLS BAG and place it on that exquisitely crafted model of Susan, my devoted and faithful moggy. Now, TWEAK the MOTION RECORDER, and select RECORD. Using the cursor, select the MOTION RECORDER by holding down the T BUTTON and waggle it around until you or Susan throw up because of all the G-forces and the science. Simply release the T BUTTON when you're done, and the motion is recorded! Play it back by simply UNPAUSING the game. Well I never - like a cat on a hot tin roof on a pogo stick. Try holding your MOTION CONTROLLER upright. This makes the MOTION RECORDER track the POSITION of the MOTION CONTROLLER instead of just the angle! To replay your recording endlessly, set LOOPING to YES. But that's not all! You can play your recording FORWARDS, BACKWARDS or even FORWARDS THEN BACKWARDS. And of course you can watch it over and over again as fast or as slow as you like by TWEAKING the SPEED. To make your recording loop from exactly the place it started press the CROSS BUTTON during the recording to activate EXACT LOOPING. Return the object back to the GREEN CIRCLE at the start and you will be rewarded most handsomely! Well, you'll get an exact loop, just as the name implies. One last thing - you can record the SQUARE, TRIANGLE and MOVE BUTTONS and connect their outputs to practically anything!  Connect the MOVE BUTTON OUTPUT to dear old Susan's eyes, why don't you? Susan doesn't look well - I wonder if she's feline ok? I bet that gave her paws for thought. I ought to whisker away to... No. I draw the line at "whisker away".

2530242809: The Spinginator is a powerup that can be worn by our four-legged chum, OddSock. It’s on the Creatures & Characters page of your Tools Bag, so grab one and place it into the world with the left stick and the action button. Simply run over the Springinator pedestal as OddSock and behold! You now have stylish, bouncy behind. With the Spinginator equipped, OddSock can perform acrobatic Spring Bounces. Simply hold down the grab button whilst in the air and you’ll bounce off any surface you land on as you fall. Remember, you can only Spring Bounce off flat surfaces. No walls or steep surfaces are allowed. Wall jumping is still possible whilst wearing a Spinginator, so mix it up to reach even greater heights!  When you’re done bouncing all over the place, you can remove the Springinator with the cancel button.  You can also use the Powerup Remover to strip away the powerup from those who just don’t know when to stop. You can also make adjustments to your Springinator by opening up its tweak menu using the popit cursor and the menu button. Here, you can change the pedestal to be either dynamic or static by tweaking the Physics Properties. Use the Can Be Dropped tweak to allow or prevent players removing the powerup once they’ve equipped it.  Tweak the Bounce Strength to change the height of a Spring Bounce. The higher the number, the higher you soar! Lastly, you can tweak the Impact Strength to change how much force the Spring Bounce sends into the surface below it.  Your Bounces can be as light as a feather or as heavy as a sack full of really heavy things.

3146077102: A Rod is a connection between two objects that has a set length; objects connected by a Rod cannot move closer to or further from one another. They’re on the Gameplay page of the Tools Bag, so navigate to them with the left stick and select them with the action button. To place a connector, use the left stick to move your popit cursor to the surface of an object or material until you see it highlighted, and then press the action button to place the base. Then move your popit cursor to another surface and press the action button to place the other end. Now your two surfaces are connected! To open the Rod’s tweak menu, hover over it with the popit cursor and press the menu button. There are only a few tweaks to learn, so you should be an expert in no time!  First of all, you can shorten or lengthen the Rod’s length using the Length tweak. Just change the number with the left and right directional buttons or the left stick. Next you have the Stiff tweak. Set this to Yes and the Rod will become rigid, never shifting or twisting. Change it to No and it will instead become looser and floppier. It still won’t bend, but it’ll have a lot more give. Finally, use the Visible in Play Mode and Mute tweaks to determine whether a Rod can be seen or heard by your players!
